article_title: RRB NTPC Undergraduate vs Graduate: Posts, Salary & Pattern
meta_title: RRB NTPC Undergraduate vs Graduate: Posts, Salary & Pattern
meta_description: Compare RRB NTPC undergraduate and graduate levels: eligibility, age limit, posts, pay levels, exam pattern and job role. Find out which one suits you.
meta_keyword: RRB NTPC, RRB NTPC undergraduate vs graduate, RRB NTPC eligibility, RRB NTPC posts, RRB NTPC salary, RRB NTPC exam pattern, RRB NTPC age limit, railway NTPC graduate level, railway NTPC 12th pass, NTPC pay level, railway jobs after 12th, railway jobs for graduates

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
RRB NTPC (Non-Technical Popular Categories) is one of the most popular railway recruitments in India. It is run in two levels: one for graduates and one for 12th pass candidates. They look alike, but the age limit, posts, pay and day-to-day work are quite different. This guide puts both levels side by side, so you can see which one suits you before you read a single notification.

Railway Recruitment Boards can change posts, age limits, pay levels and the exam pattern between cycles. This article explains how the two levels normally work. For the final word on any cycle, read the official Centralised Employment Notification (CEN).

The quick comparison

Point Graduate level Undergraduate level
Qualification Bachelor's degree from a recognised university Class 12 pass or equivalent
Usual age limit 18 to 33 years 18 to 30 years
Pay levels Level 4, 5 and 6, depending on the post Level 2 and 3, depending on the post
Typical posts Goods Train Manager, Station Master, Chief Commercial-cum-Ticket Supervisor, Senior Clerk-cum-Typist, Junior Accounts Assistant-cum-Typist Commercial-cum-Ticket Clerk, Accounts Clerk-cum-Typist, Junior Clerk-cum-Typist, Trains Clerk
Selection stages CBT 1, CBT 2, skill test for some posts, document verification, medical CBT 1, CBT 2, typing test for typist posts, document verification, medical
Exam style Computer-based, objective questions Computer-based, objective questions

The age limit is counted as on a cut-off date given in each notification, not on the day you apply. Always check that date for your cycle.

Eligibility in detail

Education

Graduate posts need a degree in any stream from a recognised university. Undergraduate posts need Class 12 or an equivalent qualification. Because the undergraduate requirement is a minimum, a graduate can usually apply for undergraduate posts too, though the lower age limit of 30 still applies. Check the wording in the CEN before you decide.

Eligibility is normally judged on the qualification you hold by the last date of application. A final-year student who has not completed the degree by then generally cannot apply for graduate posts.

Age and relaxation

The upper age limit is usually 33 for graduate posts and 30 for undergraduate posts. Relaxation is given as per railway rules, which commonly means 3 years for OBC-NCL and 5 years for SC and ST candidates, with extra relaxation for persons with disabilities and ex-servicemen.

Nationality, fee and medical standards

You must be an Indian citizen, with the usual exceptions for people from Nepal and Bhutan and certain Tibetan refugees. In recent notifications, the application fee has been ₹500 for General candidates and ₹250 for SC, ST, PwBD, women, transgender candidates, ex-servicemen, minority communities and economically backward candidates.

Medical standards are different for each post. Jobs involving train safety, like Goods Train Manager and Station Master, have stricter vision and fitness rules than clerical posts. The medical category for every post is listed in the CEN.

Posts you can get

Graduate level

Post Pay level What the job is
Station Master Level 6 (₹35,400) Controls train movement at a station and is responsible for safe operation
Chief Commercial-cum-Ticket Supervisor Level 6 (₹35,400) Supervises ticketing and commercial work at stations
Goods Train Manager Level 5 (₹29,200) In charge of a goods train on the run, including safety, paperwork and coordination with control
Junior Accounts Assistant-cum-Typist Level 5 (₹29,200) Accounts and office work, with typing
Senior Clerk-cum-Typist Level 5 (₹29,200) Office clerical work, files and typing
Traffic Assistant, Senior Commercial-cum-Ticket Clerk and similar Level 4 and 5 Station and traffic work, appearing in some cycles

Not every post appears in every cycle. Some notifications cover only a few of these, so check which posts are listed before you plan around one.

Undergraduate level

Post Pay level What the job is
Commercial-cum-Ticket Clerk Level 3 (₹21,700) Booking counters, reservations and passenger queries at stations
Accounts Clerk-cum-Typist Level 2 (₹19,900) Accounts work and typing in railway offices
Junior Clerk-cum-Typist Level 2 (₹19,900) General office work and typing
Trains Clerk Level 2 (₹19,900) Records and coordination of train movement

Salary: what the pay levels mean

The basic pay for each level comes from the pay matrix of the Pay Commission in force. Railway employees get several things on top of it: Dearness Allowance (DA), House Rent Allowance (HRA) and Transport Allowance. Deductions like NPS contribution and income tax come off after that. DA is revised from time to time, and HRA depends on the class of the city you are posted in.

Pay level Starting basic pay (7th CPC) Posts that usually fall here
Level 2 ₹19,900 Junior Clerk, Accounts Clerk, Trains Clerk
Level 3 ₹21,700 Commercial-cum-Ticket Clerk
Level 4 ₹25,500 Some traffic and commercial posts
Level 5 ₹29,200 Goods Train Manager, Senior Clerk, Junior Accounts Assistant
Level 6 ₹35,400 Station Master, Chief Commercial-cum-Ticket Supervisor

To estimate your monthly gross, add DA at the current rate and HRA for your posting city to the basic pay. Your actual in-hand amount will be lower after NPS and other deductions. A posting in a metro pays more in HRA than a small town does.

The jump from Level 2 to Level 6 is large. That gap is the main reason people with a degree aim for the graduate posts. Pay levels can also be revised whenever a new Pay Commission is implemented, so treat the figures above as the current structure and not a permanent one.

Exam pattern

The selection process is built on the same stages for both levels. The exact stages depend on the post.

  1. CBT 1, a screening test
  2. CBT 2, the main test
  3. Typing skill test for typist posts, or an aptitude test for posts like Station Master and Traffic Assistant
  4. Document verification
  5. Medical examination

CBT 1

Section Questions
General Awareness 40
Mathematics 30
General Intelligence and Reasoning 30
Total 100 questions, 90 minutes

There is a negative mark of one-third for each wrong answer. CBT 1 is used to shortlist candidates for the next stage, and its marks are generally not counted in the final merit.

CBT 2

Section Questions
General Awareness 50
Mathematics 35
General Intelligence and Reasoning 35
Total 120 questions, 90 minutes

CBT 2 marks decide the merit list for most posts. Typist posts add a qualifying typing test, and posts like Station Master and Traffic Assistant add an aptitude test. After that, shortlisted candidates go through document verification and a medical. Marks in these later stages are mostly qualifying in nature, but the rules differ by post, so read them in the CEN.

The numbers above follow the standard NTPC format used in recent cycles. Check the pattern in the CEN of the cycle you are applying for, in case the board changes it.

What the job is like

The two levels feel different once you join. Graduate posts like Goods Train Manager involve duty on the run, long hours away from home and responsibility for the train and its crew. Station Masters run shifts that cover nights and holidays, because stations never close. The pay is better, but the schedule is harder.

Clerk posts, on both the graduate and undergraduate side, are mostly office jobs with more regular hours. Ticket clerks work station shifts, which can include nights and weekends. Postings are within the railway zone you are allotted, and transfers are common, especially early on. If staying in a particular city matters to you, look at the region and zone you apply under before you fill the form.

Growth after joining

Railway jobs move through promotions and departmental exams. Many people join at a lower level and move up over the years, for example from clerk posts to senior clerk or supervisor posts through seniority and exams. The speed depends on vacancies in your department, and it is generally slower than people expect, so treat the starting post as the one you will hold for a good few years.

Which level is right for you?

If you have a degree and are within the age limit, the graduate level is usually the better choice. The pay is higher, the posts are more senior, and there is more room to grow. The trade-off is that jobs like Goods Train Manager and Station Master involve irregular duty.

If you are 12th pass without a degree, the undergraduate level is your way in. It is a stable entry into the railways, and you can aim for higher posts later through departmental routes and, in the meantime, complete a degree to open the graduate level in future cycles.

If you are in the last year of your degree, remember that you may not be eligible for graduate posts until the degree is complete. Plan your attempts around that.

Some cycles have allowed candidates to apply to both levels. Read the rule in the CEN, because when it is allowed, applying to both can be a sensible backup.

Preparation: one plan works for both

The syllabus for the two levels is almost the same: General Awareness, Mathematics and Reasoning, at similar difficulty. So you do not need two separate plans.

  • Maths and reasoning together carry the most marks, so give them steady daily practice
  • For General Awareness, cover current affairs, basic science, history, geography, polity and economy, plus railway-related topics
  • Take full-length mocks in the 90 minute format and review every wrong answer
  • Watch your accuracy, because the one-third negative marking punishes blind guessing
  • If you are going for a typist post, practise typing speed early, since the typing test is qualifying

Common questions

Can a graduate apply for undergraduate posts?

Usually yes, because the requirement is a minimum of Class 12. The lower age limit of the undergraduate level will still apply.

Is the exam pattern different for graduate and undergraduate?

Not by much. The stages are the same, and the difference is mainly in the posts and the pay level. Typist posts add a typing test, and some graduate posts add an aptitude test.

Which level has better chances?

Graduate posts often have more vacancies, but many more graduates apply for them too. There is no safe way to call one easier, so prepare for the level you are eligible for.

Is the job transferable?

Yes. Railway jobs involve transfers within the zone, and sometimes beyond it, so you should be ready for postings away from home.

Will the salary change in the future?

Yes. A new Pay Commission usually revises pay levels and allowances, and DA changes from time to time. Always check the latest figures.

Final word

The choice mostly makes itself. If you have a degree and are within the age limit, the graduate level is the stronger option. If you are 12th pass, the undergraduate level is a solid start, and you can build from there. Read the CEN of the cycle you are applying for, check the eligibility line by line, and prepare for the pattern and not just the syllabus.

Preparing for RRB NTPC? Tell us which level you are going for in the comments.

article_title: UPSC vs SSC vs State PSC: Salary, Job Role & Work-Life Balance
meta_title: UPSC vs SSC vs State PSC: Salary, Job Role & Work-Life Balance
meta_description: Compare UPSC, SSC CGL and State PSC jobs by salary, job roles, posting, transfers, work-life balance, competition, age limits and career growth.
meta_keyword: UPSC vs SSC vs State PSC, UPSC vs SSC CGL, State PSC vs UPSC, UPSC salary, SSC CGL salary, State PSC salary, government jobs in India, civil services vs SSC, government job work life balance, UPSC vs State PCS

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
If you are preparing for a government job in India, sooner or later you hit the same question. Should I go for UPSC, SSC, or my state PSC?

Most articles on this topic give you a neat table and call it a day. The real difference shows up after you join. It shows up in where you live, how often your bags are packed, who calls you at 11 pm, and how much of your life is still yours.

This guide covers all of that, in plain words.

The quick picture

Point UPSC (Civil Services) SSC (CGL) State PSC
Typical entry post IAS, IPS, IFS and other Group A services Inspector, Assistant Section Officer, Auditor, Tax Assistant Deputy Collector, DSP, BDO, Tehsildar and similar
Pay level at entry Level 10 (basic ₹56,100) Level 4 to Level 8 for most posts Depends on the state, often close to central levels
Competition Extreme Very high High, but varies by state
Posting All India, or your allotted state cadre Mostly central offices, many in metros Your own state only
Transfers Frequent Moderate Frequent, mostly inside the state
Work pressure Highest Moderate High in field posts

Now let's go through each one properly.

Salary: what actually reaches your bank account

Government salary has more parts than people think. Basic pay is just the start. On top of it come Dearness Allowance (DA), House Rent Allowance (HRA), and Transport Allowance. Then come the deductions, mainly NPS contribution and tax.

DA is currently 60% of basic pay for central government employees. State employees get their own DA rate, which can be higher or lower depending on the state.

UPSC (IAS, IPS and others)

A fresh officer starts at Level 10 with a basic of ₹56,100. With 60% DA added, that is roughly ₹90,000 before other allowances. The twist is that the salary is not the main thing here. Government housing, an official vehicle, staff, security in some posts, and the sheer authority of the post make the package much bigger than the number on the payslip. Salary also grows steadily, and senior officers reach the secretary level with a fixed pay far above what a fresh officer earns.

SSC CGL posting

Where you end up depends on the department. Income Tax, Customs and Excise have offices in almost every state, so you could land in Nagpur or Guwahati as easily as Delhi. Most ministry jobs, like Assistant Section Officer, sit in Delhi. You can ask for a transfer to your home region after a few years, but nobody promises it. Some people get it in five years, some wait ten.

State PSC posting

You stay in your own state, and honestly that's the biggest reason people choose this route. Your language, your food, parents a short train ride away. The catch is the first posting. New officers usually get the district nobody wants, and later transfers inside the state can come suddenly.

Work-life balance

UPSC gives you the most respect and the least free time. A DM or SP can get a call at 2 am about a riot, a bridge collapse or a minister's visit, and you go. Diwali, Eid, your sister's wedding, none of it is safe from the phone. A lot of officers say the job slowly becomes who they are. If you want evenings with your family, think twice. If you want to actually change things in a district, there's no better seat.

SSC jobs are the easy ones to live with. Most offices run on fixed hours, Saturdays and Sundays are mostly yours, and getting leave isn't a fight. The price you pay is growth. Promotions are slow, and plenty of people sit in the same grade for ten or fifteen years waiting for the next one.

State PSC lands somewhere between the two. A Tehsildar or DSP on field duty gets calls at odd hours, same as an IAS officer, just at a smaller scale. A desk job in the state secretariat is much calmer. One more thing nobody mentions in coaching ads: in some states, local politicians have a lot of say in your posting, and that can make life hard if you don't play along.

Competition and preparation time

Lakhs of people fill the UPSC form every year and only about a thousand get a post. Less than one percent make it. Most of the people who clear it needed two to four attempts, and many gave a few full years to it with no income.

SSC CGL has many more vacancies, but also a huge crowd. The paper is fast. You need to solve maths and reasoning quickly and cleanly, so most of your preparation time goes into mock tests rather than reading books.

State PSC has fewer applicants than UPSC. The syllabus is close to UPSC, with extra questions on your state's history, geography and schemes. If your state commission holds exams on time, this can be the most realistic option. But some states are famous for late results, paper leaks and court stays, so look up how your own state's commission has behaved in the last five years before you commit.

Attempts and age limit: UPSC gives general category candidates six attempts till age 32, with more attempts and age relaxation for OBC, SC, ST and some other categories. SSC CGL has no limit on attempts, but the age limit depends on the post. State PSC rules change from state to state, and many allow a higher age than UPSC. Rules change, so check the latest official notification.

Which one should you pick?

There's no single right answer. Here's how I'd think about it.

If you want power and can handle years of preparation and a life on the move, go for UPSC. If you want a steady central job with regular hours and you're fine not being the final decision-maker, SSC fits better, and it also helps if you need to start earning sooner. If staying near home matters most, and you still want a post with real responsibility, State PSC makes sense.

You don't have to pick only one. Many UPSC aspirants also write SSC and their state exam as a backup, and that works well until it starts eating into your main preparation. Then it doesn't.

Before you decide

Don't choose by salary or the name of the post alone. Picture your life ten years from now and ask which of these jobs you can actually live with.

Better still, find someone who is already in the service and ask about their worst week on the job, not their best. That one talk will tell you more than any article, this one included.

Note: Salary, DA and exam rules in this article follow the 7th Pay Commission structure and the rules at the time of writing. The 8th Pay Commission or new notifications can change them, so check official sources before you decide.

meta_keyword: laid off from bioware, bioware layoff resume, bioware laid off what to do, game industry layoff resume, game developer portfolio after layoff, laid off game developer resume, how to show NDA work in portfolio, game artist portfolio tips, game dev jobs after layoff

contents.content:
BioWare has been through layoffs more than once. In August 2023, the studio cut around 50 roles while Dragon Age: The Veilguard was still in development. In early 2025, after that game launched, there was another round, with some people moved to other EA teams and others leaving the company. If you were part of either wave, or if you come from some other studio that has done the same, this guide is for you.

It covers the first week after a layoff, what you can and cannot show from your old work, how to write a game industry resume, how to build a portfolio when your best work is under NDA, and where to look next. A lot of it is written with story-driven RPG developers in mind, because that is the kind of work BioWare people do. But the steps work for any studio and any role.

What to do in the first week

Give yourself a day or two to calm down. After that, a few things are easier to handle early, while people still answer your messages and the details are fresh.

Task Why it matters
Read your exit paperwork fully Check your last pay date, when benefits stop, and any clause about confidentiality or non-compete. If something is unclear, ask a lawyer before signing.
Ask about internal openings When BioWare announced the 2023 cuts, it said affected staff could apply for open roles at other EA studios. Ask HR if the same applies to you and what the deadline is.
Check local unemployment and benefits rules Rules and deadlines are different in every country and province. If you are in Canada, look at the federal and provincial rules for your situation, because some have short windows to apply.
Save your contacts Get personal emails or LinkedIn links of leads, producers and teammates you trust. Your work email will stop working.
Ask for references Ask now. People are usually happy to help right after a layoff.
Get your job title and dates in writing Titles in credits can change later. A short email from HR is enough proof.
Update LinkedIn Many recruiters search there first. Turn on the open to work setting.

One thing to avoid: do not copy source code, internal builds or confidential files to your personal drive, even if it feels harmless. It can lead to legal trouble, and the games industry is small. People talk.

What you can show from your BioWare work

This is the question that worries most people. You may have spent years on a game, and some of that work may never be released or may not be public yet. So where is the line?

Usually fine Check first Usually not allowed
Work from games that are already released, like Dragon Age: The Veilguard Work from a game that is announced but not out yet Anything from unreleased projects that has not been shown publicly, including early work on the next Mass Effect
Public trailers, store pages and published interviews Screenshots of internal tools or engine editors Source code and proprietary tools
Your own side projects and mods Anything you made using studio assets or on studio time Internal design documents, story bibles and builds
Your role described in simple words Sales figures, player numbers, budgets Anything covered by a clause you signed
This table is a general guide, not legal advice. Your signed contract decides what you can share. If you are not sure, email your old studio and ask before you publish anything.

A short message like this usually works: "I would like to show my work on [project name] in my portfolio. Can you tell me what is okay to share?" Most studios give a clear yes or no, and asking makes you look careful, not difficult.

Do you need to explain the layoff on your resume?

No. A resume lists roles and dates. It does not need a reason for leaving. Recruiters in games have seen layoffs many times, and a studio-wide cut says nothing bad about you.

If you still want a note, keep it to one short line, like "Role eliminated in studio restructuring". Do not write anything negative about the studio, and do not complain about it online either. Future employers read those posts.

You will likely be asked about it in interviews, so have a calm answer ready.

Sample answer: "The studio reduced its team after the game launched, and my role was one of the ones affected. I'm proud of what we shipped, and now I'm looking for a team where I can keep working on [your area]."

Say it, then go straight back to talking about your work. Do not over-explain.

Translate your BioWare experience for other studios

Years at one studio means you pick up a lot of internal language. Recruiters at other companies may not know what it means. Before you send your resume anywhere, go through it and swap studio-only words for plain ones.

  • If you worked in EA's Frostbite engine, say so, but also describe the skills in general terms, like real-time 3D, tools workflow or gameplay scripting, so people who use Unreal or Unity still see the match
  • Replace internal tool names with what the tool did, for example "dialogue authoring tool" instead of a name only your team knows
  • Explain the scale of the project, like team size and platforms, because not every reader knows how big your team was
  • Name the genre clearly, for example "story-driven single-player RPG with branching dialogue", since this is exactly what many studios are looking for

How a game industry resume is different

Hiring managers in games want to see three things quickly: what you shipped, what you personally did on it, and which tools you used. Keep it to one page. Two pages is fine if you are senior.

  • Put shipped titles first, with platform, your role and dates
  • List tools by name, like Unreal Engine, Unity, Frostbite, Maya, Blender, ZBrush, Substance Painter, Perforce or Jira, whatever fits your job
  • Add your portfolio link at the top, not at the bottom
  • Mention team size so people understand how much of the work was yours
  • Only add awards or good reviews if you worked on that part directly

The biggest fix is to write what you did, not just your job title. Here are examples that fit RPG development.

Weak line Stronger line
Responsible for environment assets. Built 40 environment props and 3 modular kits for a large RPG hub area, bringing average asset time down from 5 days to 3.
Worked on combat features. Wrote dodge and parry code for melee combat and tuned timing windows with designers over several playtests.
Wrote quest and dialogue content. Wrote 25 side quests and around 12,000 lines of branching dialogue, and helped shape the companion banter system.
Worked on game systems. Designed the ability and talent system for party members, balancing 6 character classes across 3 difficulty levels.
Tested the game. Logged over 600 bugs in one release cycle and built a regression checklist the team kept using.
Managed the schedule. Coordinated 14 people across art, design and engineering and delivered the vertical slice two weeks early.

These numbers are only examples. Use your own. If you don't remember exact figures, give an honest estimate, and never invent anything you can't explain in an interview. People in games ask follow-up questions, and made-up numbers fall apart quickly.

Portfolio: what to show for each role

A portfolio is not a folder of everything you ever made. It is a short, careful selection. Three to five strong pieces beat fifteen average ones, because a reviewer often gives you only a few minutes.

Role What to show What reviewers look at
Narrative designer or writer Branching dialogue samples, a quest outline, a short character write-up, and one piece that shows how writing supports gameplay Voice, structure, and whether choices feel meaningful
Game or systems designer 2 or 3 case studies, level or system documents, and a playable prototype if possible Reasoning and how you improved the design over time
Environment or 3D artist 3 to 5 finished scenes or assets with wireframes and breakdowns Quality, clean topology and a clear workflow
Concept artist Sketches through to final paintings, with different subjects Design thinking and range
Animator A reel under one minute, best work first Weight, timing, polish and clear credit for what you did
Programmer GitHub projects, a playable demo, readable and documented code Code quality and problem solving
QA or producer Test plans, process documents and project case studies, with confidential parts removed Organisation, communication and results

How to write a portfolio piece

A final image or video alone doesn't say much. Reviewers want to know how you got there. A simple structure works for almost every role.

  1. The goal: what was the problem or the brief
  2. Your role: what you did and what others did
  3. The process: sketches, drafts, early versions
  4. The challenge: what went wrong or what you had to change
  5. The result: the final piece and what you learned

Two or three short paragraphs and a few images are enough. Make sure the page reads well on a phone, because many recruiters open links on mobile.

What if your best work is locked under NDA?

This is very common, and you still have choices.

  • Make a small new project in your free time. Even two or three weeks of work shows you are still building
  • Write a short interactive story or dialogue demo with a free tool, which is a good fit if you are a writer or narrative designer
  • Join a game jam. Jams have fixed deadlines, which helps when motivation is low
  • Recreate a scene or concept in your own style, using your own assets
  • Write a short breakdown of a technique or system you know well
  • Contribute to a mod or an open-source tool

For NDA work, you can still describe your role and skills in general terms on the resume, and offer more detail in an interview if your contract allows it. Many hiring managers in games understand this.

Where to look for jobs

A big share of game jobs are filled through people who already know the candidate. After a layoff, many skilled people look at the same openings at the same time, so do two things together: apply, and talk to people.

  • Check EA's internal openings first if HR gave you that option, since your experience already fits
  • Check studio career pages directly, not only job aggregator sites
  • Look at studios known for story-driven RPGs and narrative games, big and small
  • Keep LinkedIn updated and switch on the open to work setting
  • Look at games-only job boards
  • Join developer groups on Discord and Slack where people post openings
  • Message former teammates who now work elsewhere and ask for a short chat, not a job
  • Go to local meetups and industry events, online or in person
  • Share your work in public, even a short post about a small thing you made
When you message an old colleague, keep it short. Something like: "Hi, hope you're doing well. I was part of the recent layoffs and I'm looking at my next step. Would you have 15 minutes for a quick chat about your team?" Asking for advice works better than asking for a job.

Other options if studio jobs are slow

Sometimes the market is just crowded. In that case, don't treat studio work as the only path. Game skills are useful in many places.

Option Why it can help
Freelance or contract work Brings income and gives you fresh portfolio pieces
Small indie studios Wider role, more ownership, and hiring is often faster
Narrative or writing work outside games Interactive fiction, audio drama, and educational content all use the same skills
Film and TV VFX, animation Real-time and 3D skills transfer well
VR, AR and simulation Many companies need people who know game engines
Engine and tools companies Hands-on game experience is useful to people building tools
Teaching or mentoring Builds your network and keeps your skills sharp
A small project of your own Slow and uncertain, but you end up with something real to show

Mistakes people make after a layoff

  • Sending the same resume to fifty studios without changing anything
  • Leaving studio-only words and internal tool names in the resume
  • Putting every project into the portfolio instead of the best few
  • Posting angry things about the old studio online
  • Waiting for the perfect game job and ignoring everything else for months
  • Skipping networking because it feels awkward
  • Using duty-style resume lines with no results or numbers
  • Sharing something under NDA without checking first

A simple 30 day plan

Week Focus
Week 1 Paperwork, benefits, contacts, references, internal openings, and confirming what you can show
Week 2 Rewrite the resume, translate studio-only words, and update LinkedIn
Week 3 Clean up the portfolio, keep the best 3 to 5 pieces, write short case studies
Week 4 Start applying, message contacts, and begin one small new project

It won't all go on schedule, and that's fine. The point is to always know your next small step.

Look after your head too

You'll hear "stay positive" a lot, and it doesn't help much. Small habits do more. Keep a basic routine so the days don't blur together. Talk to others who were laid off, because they understand it better than most. Set a small daily goal, like one application and one message to a person, instead of a huge list. And if the stress feels heavy or doesn't ease, talk to a friend, a counsellor or a doctor. A layoff says something about a company's plans and budget. It doesn't say anything about your talent.

Common questions

Should I mention BioWare by name on my resume?

Yes. A shipped game from a well-known studio is a strong line. Just make sure your description is about your own work, in plain words.

Should I mention the layoff in my cover letter?

Usually not. Use the space to talk about the job and your best work. Bring it up only if the company asks.

How long does it take to find a new job in games?

It varies a lot by role, location and how many people are looking at the same time. It can take a few months, so plan your money for that. Do not count on getting a job in two weeks.

Can I show work from a game that is still unreleased?

Only if it has been shown publicly and your contract allows it. If it has not been announced or shown, assume you need written permission first.

Should I take a non-games job for now?

If you need the income, yes. It does not hurt your career. Keep building your portfolio on the side, so you are ready when a games role comes up.

Is freelancing a good bridge?

For many people, yes. It brings in some money, gives you new work to show and keeps you in touch with the industry. Just make sure it does not take over all the time you need for job hunting.

Final thoughts

A layoff is hard, and nobody expects you to feel fine about it, even if the studio was kind in how it handled things. But the practical work is not complicated. Sort out your paperwork, rewrite your resume around what you actually did, keep your portfolio small and clean, and talk to people. Do a little each day. That is usually enough to get moving again.

Were you affected by a studio layoff? Share what helped you most in the comments, it could help someone going through the same thing right now.

meta_keyword: indian cv to us resume, how to convert indian cv to us resume, us resume format for indians, indian resume vs us resume, what to remove from indian cv for us jobs, resume for us jobs from india, us resume tips for indian professionals, indian cv mistakes for us jobs, how to write a us style resume

category.article_description: Expert tips and useful guidance to help you create a professional, ATS-friendly resume and improve your chances of getting hired.

contents.content:
Lots of Indian professionals apply to US companies, hear nothing back, and decide that Indian experience just doesn't count abroad. Mostly that's not what's going on. The resume was written for an Indian reader, and a US recruiter who gives it under a minute can't find the point of it.

Four years at a good company, solid skills, real projects, and the document still gets skipped. It happens a lot, and it's fixable. This guide goes through what to cut, what to rewrite and how the final file should look.

Same name, different document

In India, a CV tends to be a record of the whole person. Family details, school marks, every course, every duty. A US resume is closer to a short pitch. One page (two if you're ten years in), and every line is there to make someone pick up the phone.

Item Usual Indian CV US resume
Length 2 to 4 pages 1 page, 2 for senior people
Photo Often there Not there
Personal details Date of birth, marital status, father's name, nationality None
Opening Objective, or a block of personal info Short professional summary
Education Class 10, 12 and graduation, with all marks Highest degree, maybe one more
Job entries Duties and responsibilities Results, with numbers
Salary CTC and notice period, sometimes Never
Ending Declaration and signature It just ends
Spelling British (organisation, programme) American (organization, program)
Page size A4 US Letter, 8.5 by 11 inches

Cut first, write later

Start by deleting. It's the quickest improvement you'll make, and it takes ten minutes.

US employers are expected to keep age, marital status, religion and national origin out of hiring decisions. So a recruiter who sees them on your page may feel uneasy, and some will simply set the resume aside. The photo works the same way. In India it looks normal. In the US it looks odd, and it gives the company something to worry about.

Take out the photo, date of birth, gender, marital status, father's name, religion and nationality. Cut your full home address and keep just the city and state, or city and country. Remove the declaration paragraph and the signature at the bottom. Remove class 10 and 12 marks, since nobody in Texas knows what 94% CBSE means. Remove CTC, expected salary and notice period. "References available on request" can go too, because everyone assumes it.

Hobbies are mostly dead weight as well. "Reading, music, travelling" tells a recruiter nothing. The exception is a hobby that connects to the job, like running a coding blog or coaching a football team, and then one short line is enough.

This is general guidance, not legal advice. Practices differ between companies, but leaving these details out is the safe choice almost every time.

Rewrite the summary and the bullets

The old "seeking a challenging role in a dynamic organization" objective has been read ten thousand times, so skip it. Write two or three lines instead: who you are, how many years you've worked, what you're good at, and the role you want. Specific beats polished.

The bullets are where most people lose the recruiter. Indian CVs are full of duties, like "responsible for developing modules" or "involved in testing and deployment". Fine, but did it go well? Did anything change because you were there? A US resume wants the outcome. Begin with a strong verb, say what you did, and add a number if you have one.

Usual Indian style US style
Responsible for developing backend modules for client's banking application. Built 6 Spring Boot services for a retail banking app (around 2M customers). Tuned the slow queries and cut average response time by roughly 18%.
Involved in testing and deployment activities. Wrote automated regression tests and caught 40+ bugs before release. Releases now take 1 day, they used to take 2.
Worked closely with team members to meet deadlines. Led a team of 4 on the payments upgrade. Shipped 2 weeks before the deadline.
Handled customer queries and escalations. Closed 60+ tickets a day, 95% customer satisfaction.

No exact figures? An estimate is fine. "About 30 users" or "roughly 15% faster" reads normally. Just don't write anything you couldn't explain out loud, because the interviewer will ask.

Explain what a US reader won't know

A company that's famous in India may mean nothing in Ohio. Add a few words after the name, like "Nexora Systems (IT services, about 3,000 employees)", so the reader gets the scale at a glance.

Money needs the same treatment. Lakh and crore don't register outside India, so convert roughly to dollars and write something like "managed a budget of about $480K". Do the same for degrees: write the full name, and show your grade with its scale, like GPA 8.1/10. Don't turn it into a 4.0 yourself. Different formulas give different answers, and if a company needs an official evaluation, it will ask.

What we usually write What to write instead
Fresher Entry-level
B.Tech / B.E. Bachelor of Technology / Bachelor of Engineering
CGPA 8.1 GPA 8.1/10
Lakh / Crore Approximate USD, or "INR 4 crore (about $480K)"
Notice period Leave it out
Passed out in 2020 Graduated 2020
Organisation, programme, centre Organization, program, center
Mobile no. Phone: +91 98765 43210

The layout matters more than you'd think

An Indian resume can look perfect to you and still fall apart in the software many US companies use to read applications. Those systems read one line at a time, top to bottom, so columns, sidebars, text boxes, icons and skill bars can scramble your content.

Use one column and a plain font like Arial, Calibri or Times New Roman at 10 to 12 pt. Stick to ordinary headings: Summary, Experience, Education, Skills. Put your latest job first and write dates the same way throughout, like Jun 2021 to Present. Switch the page to US Letter, because an A4 file can shift its margins when someone opens or prints it on a US system. Save it as a text-based PDF with a normal name, like Priya_Nair_Resume.pdf, not final_final2.pdf.

For most experienced people, the order is header (name, city, phone, email, LinkedIn), summary, skills, experience, education, and then extras like certifications. Freshers and recent graduates usually put education above experience.

Sample: before and after

The sample below is a made-up candidate with four years as a software engineer in Bengaluru, applying for US roles. First, the "before".

Section Before (Indian CV)
Top PRIYA K NAIR (photo pasted on the right side). D.O.B :- 04-08-1998. Sex :- Female. Marital status :- Unmarried. Father's name :- Mr. Krishnan Nair. Nationality :- Indian. Languages known :- English, Hindi & Malayalam. Mob :- 98765 43210. Address :- Flat no 302, Sai Residency, 2nd cross HSR layout, Bangalore 560102
Objective Career Objective :- To obtain a challenging position in a reputed organization wherein I can utilize my skill & knowledge for the growth of the organization and my self.
Education B.E. (Computer Science) - Kaveri Institute of Technology, Bangalore (VTU) - 2020 - 8.1 CGPA
12th - PUC, Karnataka Board - 2016 - 92%
10th - CBSE - 2014 - 94%
Experience Working as Software Engineer in Nexora Systems Pvt Ltd, Bangalore since June 2020.
Roles and responsibilities: developing backend modules in Java for banking client, bug fixing and testing, deployment support, attending client calls and daily status meetings.

And here is the rewrite.

Section After (US resume)
Header Priya Nair | Bengaluru, India | +91 98765 43210 | priya.nair@email.com | linkedin.com/in/priyanair
Summary Java developer with 4 years on a retail banking platform at Nexora Systems. Most of my work is Spring Boot services and the APIs they expose. Looking for backend roles in the US. Open to relocation.
Skills Java 8/11, Spring Boot, Hibernate, MySQL, Oracle, REST APIs, Kafka, JUnit, Selenium, Git, Jenkins, Docker
Experience Software Engineer, Nexora Systems (IT services, about 3,000 employees), Bengaluru. Jun 2020 to Present
- Built 6 Spring Boot services for a retail banking app (around 2M customers)
- Rewrote the slowest SQL queries on the statement API and added caching. Average response time down by roughly 18%
- Wrote regression tests in JUnit and Selenium. 40+ bugs caught before release
- Led a team of 4 on the payments upgrade, shipped 2 weeks before the deadline
Education B.E., Computer Science. Kaveri Institute of Technology (VTU), Bengaluru, India. GPA 8.1/10, 2020

Same person, same four years. The photo, birth date, family details, school marks and the objective line are gone. A recruiter can now see in a few seconds what she works on and what she changed.

Visa and work authorization

If you're applying from India and would need sponsorship, don't hide it and don't lie about it. Some US employers sponsor visas and a lot don't, and the application form will usually ask you straight. Writing "Open to relocation" on the resume, or stating your status on the form, is fine as long as it's true. If you're already in the US on a student or work visa, check the rules for your specific status before you decide how to describe it.

Visa rules change often. Check official government sources or talk to an immigration lawyer before you make decisions based on your status.

LinkedIn and the cover letter

The resume is only part of it. Update your LinkedIn so it matches, with a clear headline. It's also the one place where a professional photo is normal. If the job allows a cover letter, keep it short and specific to that company. Sending the same generic letter to fifty places rarely works.

Keep one base resume and adjust the summary and the order of your skills for each posting. Use words from the job description where they're true for you, and leave out the ones that aren't.

A few questions people ask

Should I keep my class 10 and 12 marks?

No. Put your highest degree, and one more if it matters. School marks take up room and mean little to a US recruiter.

Is a two-page resume ever okay?

Yes, if you have around ten years of experience and the second page has real content on it. If it's only filler, cut it.

What about languages I speak?

Add them to the skills section if they help for the job. Otherwise skip them.

Should I put my Indian phone number?

Yes, with the +91 country code. If you have a number that works for calls or messages from the US, add that as well.

Do I list projects?

If you have little work experience, yes. A couple of good projects with the tools and results can balance a short history. With several years behind you, they matter less.

Before you hit apply

Check Done?
No photo, date of birth, marital status, father's name or declaration ☐
One page, or two only if you really need it ☐
A summary instead of the old objective ☐
Bullets show results, with numbers where you have them ☐
Company context and dollar figures added where needed ☐
American spelling, Letter size, single column ☐
LinkedIn updated to match ☐

Your experience doesn't lose value when it crosses a border. It just has to be shown the way the other side expects. Do the cutting, rewrite the bullets around results, fix the format, and the same career looks a lot stronger on one clean page.

Moving from an Indian CV to a US resume right now? Tell us which part is confusing you in the comments, and we'll try to help.

category.article_description: Expert tips and useful guidance to help you create a professional, ATS-friendly resume and improve your chances of getting hired.

contents.content:
Many freshers in India send out fifty or sixty applications and hear back from almost nobody. The usual reaction is to blame the job market, the college tag, or luck. Sometimes that is fair. But very often the real problem is much smaller: the resume is hard for software to read.

This guide explains how applicant tracking systems (ATS) actually work, what a safe resume layout looks like, where to find the right keywords, and what to remove from the old biodata-style resume. At the end there is a sample resume, before and after, so you can see the difference line by line.

What an ATS really is

You may have heard that an ATS is a robot that throws your resume in the bin. That is not quite true. And videos that promise a "95% ATS score" are mostly trying to sell you something.

An ATS is basically a database for recruiters. When you apply, it pulls the text out of your file, tries to sort it into fields like name, education, skills and experience, and stores it. Later, a recruiter searches it with words like "Python", "B.Tech" or "Pune". If your details went into the wrong field, or did not come out at all, you will not show up in that search. Nobody rejected you. You were just never seen.

Some companies also set hard filters, like a minimum percentage or a graduation year. So those details matter too.

Where Indian freshers will meet an ATS

  • Job portals like Naukri, Foundit and LinkedIn, which have their own resume parsers
  • Career pages of bigger companies, which often run on tools like Workday or Greenhouse
  • Campus hiring portals, where your uploaded resume is stored and searched
  • Small startups, which may just read resumes in email, but a clean layout helps there as well

Keep the layout boring

Software reads one line at a time, from top to bottom. Anything that makes it jump around, like columns, sidebars and text boxes, causes trouble. Boring layouts win.

Element Safe choice Risky choice
Layout One column Two or three columns, sidebars
Font Arial, Calibri or Times New Roman, 10 to 12 pt Handwriting style fonts
Headings Education, Projects, Skills, Internships "My Journey", "What I Bring"
Graphics None Icons, skill bars, pie charts
Photo Leave it out Passport photo in the corner
Contact details In the main body of the page Only in the page header
File type Text-based PDF or .docx, whichever the company asks for A PDF that is really a flat image
File name Rahul_Verma_Resume.pdf resume_final_v3_new.pdf
Length One page Two pages with school-level details
30 second test: open your PDF, select all, copy, and paste into Notepad. If the order is wrong or something is missing, the parser will have the same problem.

Old biodata habits to drop

A lot of Indian resumes still follow the old biodata style. It worked for a different time. Today it takes space and adds nothing.

  • Remove the photo, date of birth, father's name, religion, marital status and caste
  • Delete the "I hereby declare that the above information is true" line at the bottom
  • Replace "Seeking a challenging role in a reputed organisation" with a real two-line summary
  • Write your phone number in a clear format like +91 98765 43210
  • Give your city and state, since recruiters filter by location, but skip your full home address
  • Write your CGPA or percentage the way your university gives it, and mention which one it is
  • Do not list "MS Office" and "Internet" as skills, because everyone is assumed to have them

Where keywords come from

Keywords are just the words the employer used to describe the job. So your source is the job posting itself. Read it twice, notice which words repeat, and if you honestly have those skills, use the same words in your resume.

  1. Copy the job description into a notepad
  2. Underline the tools, skills and qualifications that appear more than once
  3. Check which of them you really have
  4. Add those words to your summary, projects and skills section, where they fit naturally
Fresher role Words you often see in job postings
Software developer Java, Python, SQL, OOP, data structures, Git, REST API
Data analyst Excel, SQL, Power BI, Tableau, data cleaning, dashboards
Digital marketing SEO, Google Analytics, Google Ads, social media, email campaigns
Accounts and finance Tally, GST, bookkeeping, reconciliation, Excel
HR and recruitment Sourcing, screening, onboarding, ATS, communication
Customer support CRM, ticketing, English and Hindi, typing speed, query resolution
Sales and business development Lead generation, client communication, CRM, negotiation

Use this as a rough guide, not a list to copy. The job posting in front of you always matters more than any table.

Do not paste fifty keywords in white font at the bottom of the page. Recruiters notice it, newer systems flag it, and it can get your application dropped. Use only words for skills you actually have.

How to write each section

Summary

Two lines are enough. Say your degree, your main skills, and the kind of role you want. Skip words like "hardworking" and "passionate", because everyone writes them.

Education

Write the degree, college, city, years and CGPA or percentage in one or two lines. For a fresher, 12th and 10th marks can be one short line each, or left out if your graduation marks are strong and the form does not ask.

Projects

For freshers, projects are the main proof of skill. A simple formula works well for each project.

  1. Name of the project and the tools used
  2. The problem it solved
  3. What you built
  4. A result, even a small one, like number of users or time saved

Skills

Group skills by type, like languages, tools and concepts. Do not use percentage bars or star ratings. They mean nothing to software, and a person cannot tell what "60% in Java" is supposed to show.

Internships, certificates and extras

List internships with the company, duration and what you actually did. Add only certificates that match the role. If you have no internship, college club work, hackathons, volunteering and freelance tasks can fill that space, as long as you describe what you did in plain words.

Sample resume: before and after

The sample below uses a made-up candidate. The "before" version has problems that appear on many fresher resumes.

Section Before
Top of page [Passport photo] RAHUL VERMA. Date of Birth: 12/03/2002. Father's Name: Mr. S. K. Verma. Religion: Hindu. Marital Status: Unmarried. Full home address with pin code
Objective Seeking a challenging position in a reputed organisation where I can utilise my skills and grow with the company.
Skills Python ■■■■□ (80%), Java ■■■□□ (60%), Hardworking, Team player, MS Office, Internet, Quick learner
Projects Library Management System. College Website.
Education Inside a coloured sidebar, with class 10, 12 and graduation marks in a small table
End of page Declaration: I hereby declare that all the above information is true to the best of my knowledge.

What is wrong with it:

  • The photo and family details do nothing for a recruiter
  • The objective could belong to any candidate
  • Skill bars mean nothing to software or to people
  • The projects are just two titles, with no tools or results
  • The coloured sidebar may turn into scrambled text after parsing
  • A recruiter searching for "SQL" or "Java developer" would probably never find this resume
Section After
Header Rahul Verma | Pune, Maharashtra | +91 98765 43210 | rahul.verma@email.com | linkedin.com/in/rahulverma | github.com/rahulverma
Summary Computer Science graduate with hands-on experience in Java, Python and SQL through two complete projects, looking for a junior software developer role where I can write production code and learn from experienced engineers.
Education B.Tech, Computer Science. XYZ Institute of Technology, Pune. 2020 to 2024. CGPA 8.1 out of 10
Projects Library Management System (Java, MySQL): built a desktop app to issue and return books and track late fines, replacing a paper register. About 500 books and 200 members entered. Department Website (HTML, CSS, JavaScript): six pages covering notices, faculty, timetable and contact, working on mobile too.
Skills Languages: Java, Python, SQL. Web: HTML, CSS, JavaScript. Tools: Git, GitHub, MySQL, VS Code. Concepts: Object-Oriented Programming, Data Structures, REST APIs
Internship Software Intern, ABC Tech (6 weeks): fixed 12 front-end bugs and wrote unit tests for a billing module
Certifications Java Programming Masterclass (Udemy), SQL for Data Analysis

The candidate's marks, projects and internship are exactly the same in both versions. Only the writing changed. The keywords now sit where a search can find them, the projects say what was built and what it replaced, and the page is plain enough for any parser to read.

How to test your resume before sending

  1. Do the Notepad paste test described above
  2. Open the job posting and check that the repeated words show up in your resume, but only for skills you really have
  3. Keep your phone number and email in the body of the page, not in a header
  4. Write dates in one format everywhere, like Jun 2023 to Aug 2023
  5. Open the file on your phone, because many recruiters first see it there
  6. Ask a senior or friend to look at it for two minutes and tell you what they noticed first

Common mistakes

  • Using a beautiful free template that turns into a mess when read as text
  • Hiding keywords in white font
  • Sending the same resume to every company without checking the job posting
  • Uploading a PDF that is really a flat image with no text in it
  • Listing skills you cannot talk about in an interview
  • Writing a long paragraph of duties instead of short lines with results

Last check before you hit send

Check Done?
One column, standard headings, plain font ☐
No photo, date of birth, father's name or declaration ☐
Keywords from the posting used naturally, only where true ☐
Projects say what you built, with what, and the result ☐
Sensible file name and the file type they asked for ☐
Read once, out loud, for typos ☐

Common questions

Do I need a different resume for every job?

Not a full rewrite. Keep one base resume and change the summary and the skills order to match each posting. That takes ten minutes and makes a real difference.

PDF or Word, which one is better?

Use whatever the company asks for. If nothing is mentioned, a text-based PDF is usually safe. Just make sure you can select and copy the text from it.

Is one page enough for a fresher?

Yes. A fresher with school and college details, a couple of projects and one internship fits easily on one page. A second page usually just adds filler.

Can I use a Canva template?

You can, but be careful. Many Canva templates use columns, icons and text boxes, which are exactly what parsers struggle with. If you use one, pick a single-column design, remove the graphics and run the Notepad test.

Are paid ATS score checkers worth it?

Treat the scores with caution. Every real system works differently, so no single score tells you how a company's software will read your file. A clean layout, honest keywords and the Notepad test give you more than a number.

Should I put my CGPA if it is low?

If the job posting asks for a minimum score, you need to state it honestly. If it does not, focus on your projects and skills, but do not lie or hide it when someone asks directly.

Final thoughts

An ATS-friendly resume is not a trick. It is simply a resume that a machine and a tired recruiter can both read without effort. Fix the layout, remove the old biodata habits, use honest keywords and write your projects with real results. After that, you are judged on your skills, and that is something you can keep improving.

Did changing your resume improve your replies? Tell us what you changed in the comments, it might help another fresher.

article_title: How to Handle a Difficult Boss (Without Losing Your Mind or Your Job)
meta_title: How to Handle a Difficult Boss (Without Losing Your Mind or Your Job)
meta_description: Struggling with a difficult boss? Learn how to spot the type, communicate better, protect yourself, and know when to escalate to HR or move on, with ready-to-use phrases.
meta_keyword: how to handle a difficult boss, how to deal with a bad boss, micromanager boss tips, toxic boss at work, how to talk to your boss about problems, boss takes credit for my work, when to report your boss to HR, how to survive a difficult manager, workplace stress and bad manager

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
Early in my career I had a manager who'd send me messages at 11 pm saying "call me." No context, no subject, just that. I'd spend the next half hour imagining everything I might have done wrong, then call, and it would be about a font in a presentation. This happened about twice a week for most of a year.

I used to think the answer was to work harder. Reply faster, polish everything, never give him a reason to be annoyed. It didn't work, of course. It just made me tired, and him no different. What finally helped wasn't a magic phrase, it was understanding why he behaved that way and changing how I responded, bit by bit.

If you're dealing with a boss who makes work harder than it needs to be, this is for you. Fair warning, it isn't all "just communicate better." Some bosses can be managed and some can't, and I'll try to be honest about where that line is.

First, figure out what kind of difficult it is

"Difficult" covers a lot. A boss who's disorganised needs a different approach than one who takes credit for your work, and both are different from one who's openly disrespectful. Before you do anything, it helps to name what's actually happening, because the fix depends on it.

Type What it looks like What usually helps
The micromanager Checks everything, wants constant updates, redoes your work Update them before they ask, so they stop feeling the need to check
The disorganised boss Changes priorities daily, unclear instructions, last-minute requests Confirm priorities in writing, ask "what should I drop?"
The credit taker Presents your ideas as theirs Share your work in writing and in front of others, keep a record
The absent boss Hard to reach, no direction, no feedback Book regular short check-ins, ask direct questions
The mood-swinger Friendly one day, cold or angry the next Stay calm, pick your timing, don't take it personally
The critic Only points out mistakes, never says what went well Ask for specific feedback, and ask what "good" looks like
The bully Insults, humiliates, threatens, shouts This isn't a style problem. Document it and use the formal route

Notice the last row. There's a difference between a boss who's hard to work with and a boss who's abusive. The first you can manage. The second isn't your job to fix, and I'll come back to that.

Try to understand where they're coming from

This doesn't mean excusing bad behaviour. It means looking for the pattern, because patterns can be handled. A micromanager is often under pressure from their own boss and afraid of being blamed. A disorganised boss may be overloaded and drowning. A credit taker might be insecure about their own position. Once you see the fear or pressure underneath, their behaviour becomes more predictable, and predictable is much easier to work with.

You don't need to be a psychologist. Just ask yourself: what is this person worried about, and what would make that worry smaller? Often the answer points straight to a fix.

Learn how they like to work

Some bosses want a quick message, others want a face-to-face chat. Some want details, some want just the headline. Some like surprises about as much as they like root canals. Pay attention for a couple of weeks. When do they seem most open? How do they prefer to get updates? What annoys them in a report?

Then adapt. It sounds like you're bending over backwards, but it's really just removing small friction. A boss who gets information the way they like it tends to relax a bit, and a relaxed boss is usually a better boss.

Get clear about what they actually want

A huge amount of boss-related frustration comes from unclear expectations. You think you did what was asked, they think you didn't, and both of you are annoyed. Fix this early.

  • Repeat the task back: "So you'd like the report by Thursday, covering sales and returns, in the usual format. Is that right?"
  • Ask what success looks like before you start, not after
  • If priorities change, ask directly, "Should this come before the other project?"
  • Send a short follow-up message after a verbal instruction, confirming what you understood

That last one matters more than it seems. It's not about distrust, it's about having something to point to if the instructions later change or get forgotten.

Keep a record, quietly

I'm not suggesting you turn into a detective, but a simple log of important things protects you. Dates of key conversations, what was agreed, your achievements, any incidents that crossed a line. Keep it factual, no commentary, and keep it somewhere personal, not on a company laptop.

If things never escalate, it costs you nothing. If they do, a clear record is worth far more than "he always does this."

How to actually say things

A lot of conflict gets worse because of how things are said, not what's being said. A few small shifts help a lot. Pick a calm moment, not right after a blow-up. Describe what happened and its effect, rather than attacking the person. And offer a solution, not just a complaint.

Situation Instead of this Try this
Constant last-minute requests "You always give me work at the last minute." "When tasks come in late in the day, I struggle to do them well. Could we plan the week on Monday so I can see what's coming?"
Micromanagement "You don't trust me." "I'd like to send you a short update each afternoon so you always know where things stand. Would that work?"
Credit being taken "You stole my idea." "I'd like to present this one to the team myself, since I did the groundwork."
Vague feedback "You never tell me what you want." "Could you tell me what would make this a strong piece of work, so I can aim for it?"
Being shouted at Shouting back "I want to get this right, but I can't talk about it like this. Can we continue in ten minutes?"
Unfair workload "I have too much." "I'm handling A, B and C right now. If you add D, which one should I move or drop?"

The point of these isn't to be sneaky. It's to make it easy for your boss to say yes, and hard for the problem to hide behind emotions.

Protect your own head

This part gets ignored. Working under a difficult boss wears you down in ways you don't always notice, until you realise you've been dreading Monday since Thursday. A few things genuinely help:

  • Don't carry work stress into your whole evening, if you can help it. A short walk or a call to a friend after work breaks the loop.
  • Have people you can vent to who aren't in your office. Complaining in office chats can come back to bite you.
  • Remember it's about their behaviour, not your worth. A harsh boss isn't automatically a correct one.
  • Build things outside work that feel good, whether that's a hobby, exercise or time with family.
  • If it's affecting your sleep, health or mood badly, take that seriously and talk to someone you trust or a professional.

When talking to your boss doesn't work

You've tried to adapt, you've clarified expectations, you've had the calm conversation, and nothing changes. At that point you've got a few routes, and none of them are failures.

Option When it makes sense Things to watch
Talk to your boss's manager The problem is affecting your work or the team, and you've already tried to fix it directly Stick to facts and examples, not complaints about personality
Go to HR Harassment, discrimination, bullying, unfair treatment, or policy violations Bring your record. Remember HR protects the company, so be clear and factual
Request a transfer or team change The company is fine, but this specific reporting line isn't Frame it around growth and fit, not blaming your boss
Find a mentor or sponsor elsewhere You can tolerate the boss but need guidance and visibility Don't rely on only one person for your career
Start looking for a new job The behaviour is constant, your health is suffering, and nothing's changed Look quietly, keep performing, and don't resign in anger

The line that shouldn't be crossed

Some behaviour isn't "difficult." It's unacceptable: threats, humiliation in front of others, discrimination, sexual harassment, retaliation for raising concerns. If this is what you're facing, you don't need to find a better way of communicating with them. Document what happened, with dates and witnesses if there are any, use your company's complaint process or an internal committee where one exists, and consider getting legal advice. In India, for example, workplaces are required to have an internal committee for sexual harassment complaints. If you're in serious distress, please talk to someone you trust, today.

Know when leaving is the right call

There's a lot of advice out there that says to stick it out and "learn from tough bosses." Sometimes that's true. Sometimes it's just a way of making you feel bad for wanting to go. If you've genuinely tried, and the environment is hurting your health, confidence or career, leaving is a reasonable decision, not a weakness.

If you do leave, do it well. Line up the next job first if you can, keep your work professional until the end, and don't burn bridges in the exit interview. Gossip travels, and industries are smaller than they look.

What I took away from my own experience

That manager with the 11 pm messages? Things improved a bit once I started sending a short end-of-day update without being asked. The random "call me" messages dropped by about half. Not because I'd fixed him, but because I'd removed the anxiety that made him reach out. I still left that job eventually, and I don't regret it. But I took something useful from it: most difficult bosses are managing their own stress, and you can sometimes ease it, but you aren't obliged to absorb all of it.

Have you dealt with a difficult boss? Tell me what worked for you in the comments, someone reading may be going through the same thing right now.

article_title: How to Get a Job With No Experience
meta_title: How to Get a Job With No Experience
meta_description: No experience and no job yet? Learn how to pick a direction, build proof, use referrals and cold messages, and land your first job with a realistic step-by-step plan.
meta_keyword: how to get a job with no experience, jobs for freshers with no experience, how to get your first job, entry level jobs with no experience, first job tips for freshers, how to get a job as a fresher, no experience job search, how to get an internship with no experience, fresher job search plan

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
There's a joke every fresher eventually hears: "Jobs need experience, and experience needs a job." It's funny for about a week. After that, when you've sent forty applications and got two automated replies, it stops being funny and starts feeling like a trap.

It isn't a trap, though. It just looks like one from the outside. Companies hire people with no experience all the time. Every office you've ever walked into is full of people who were once beginners and got a chance. The difference is how they went about it, and that's mostly what I want to talk about here. Not "10 secret hacks," just what actually seems to work.

Start by dropping one idea

The idea is that you should apply to hundreds of jobs and wait. That approach is slow and brutal for beginners, because on paper you lose to almost everyone. A resume with no experience, sent into a pile of two hundred, rarely wins.

What works better is a smaller number of targeted attempts, plus doing something that gives you a reason to be taken seriously. Proof, basically. Even a little. Once you have it, the same resume starts getting answers.

Pick a direction first

"I'll do anything" sounds flexible, but it reads as unfocused, and it makes your own search harder because you don't know what to learn or where to look. Choose one or two roles you'd actually be happy doing, even if it's only for the first year. You can change later. People do it constantly.

If you don't know where to start, look at which entry-level roles are easiest to get into without experience and what they ask for.

Entry-level role What they usually want How to prepare quickly
Customer support / voice process Clear communication, patience, typing speed Practise speaking and typing, learn basic CRM tools
Sales / business development trainee Confidence, persuasion, willingness to hear "no" Practise pitching, learn the product basics
Data entry / back office Accuracy, Excel basics, speed Learn Excel formulas, practise typing tests
Digital marketing trainee Social media sense, writing, basic SEO or ads Run your own page or blog, finish a free course
Content writer / intern Clear writing, research Write 3 to 5 samples and post them online
Junior developer / QA tester Fundamentals, small projects Build 2 to 3 projects and put them on GitHub
Accounts assistant Tally, Excel, basic accounting Learn Tally and GST basics, do a short course
HR assistant / recruiter trainee Communication, organisation Learn how hiring works, practise screening calls
Graphic design intern A portfolio more than anything Make 5 to 8 clean designs in Canva or Figma

Build proof, because it replaces experience

This is the whole game, honestly. Experience is just proof that you can do the work. If you don't have a job to prove it, make proof some other way.

A short course helps, but only if you finish it and do something with it. A certificate on its own is weak. A certificate plus a small project is much better. If you're learning data analysis, analyse a public dataset and write up what you found. If you want to be a content writer, write real pieces. If it's design, redesign a local shop's menu and post the before and after. It doesn't have to be impressive, just real and visible.

Instead of this Try this
Starting five courses and leaving them half done Finishing one course and building something with it
Saying "I'm a quick learner" Showing a project you learned something new to build
Listing skills with no evidence Linking to a portfolio, GitHub or sample work
Waiting for a job to gain experience Doing a small free project for a local business or friend
Applying blindly everywhere Applying to roles that match what you've proved

Take the in-between routes seriously

A lot of people skip internships because they think they're only for students or that they won't pay. Yes, some are unpaid or low-paid, and I'm not saying work for free forever. But a few months of real work gives you something to write on your resume, a reference, and a way into the company itself. Many full-time offers start as internships or trainee roles.

The same goes for apprenticeships, contract work, part-time roles and temporary jobs. A less glamorous first job that gives you real exposure beats waiting a year for the perfect one. And there's no rule that says your first job decides your whole career. It doesn't.

Referrals do more than portals

Job portals are fine, and you should use them, but they're also where the competition is highest. A referral gets your resume in front of a human, often skipping the first filter entirely. And you're probably closer to a referral than you think.

Talk to seniors from your college, friends who already work, relatives, former teachers, anyone you've met at a workshop. Don't ask "can you get me a job?" That puts people on the spot. Ask for advice instead: "I'm trying to start in marketing, what would you look at if you were me?" People like giving advice, and good conversations often turn into "send me your resume."

Reaching out to people you don't know

This is the part that scares most beginners, and it's also the part that quietly works. A short, polite message on LinkedIn to someone who works in a role or company you like. Not a copy-paste essay, just a few honest lines.

Message part Example
Who you are "Hi Priya, I'm a recent B.Com graduate learning Tally and GST."
Why them "I saw you work in accounts at a company I really admire."
A small, specific ask "Could you spare 10 minutes to tell me what skills matter most for someone starting out?"
Easy way out "No worries if you're busy, thanks for reading."

Most won't reply. Some will. And one useful reply is worth ten ignored applications. Don't ask for a job in the first message, that's the fastest way to get ignored.

Get your resume and profile ready

Your resume should be one page, built around your projects, education and skills, and tailored to the kind of role you're going after. Your LinkedIn profile needs a clear photo, a headline that says more than "Looking for opportunities," and a short summary. Recruiters check it, often before the resume. If you've got a portfolio or GitHub, link to it in both places.

It's also worth tweaking your resume a little for each job, using words from the posting where they honestly apply.

Interviews when you have no experience

Interviewers hiring beginners know you have no history. They're checking different things: do you communicate clearly, are you honest, are you teachable, and do you actually want this job. So the weak spot to avoid is sounding like you're there for any job at all.

  • Learn a bit about the company and the role, and have one real reason you want it
  • Prepare to talk about your projects in detail, including what went wrong and what you learned
  • Practise the "tell me about yourself" answer out loud until it's under two minutes
  • Be honest about what you don't know, and say how you'd find out
  • Ask one or two thoughtful questions at the end

Honesty goes a long way here. "I haven't done that before, but here's how I'd approach it" beats a bluff every time.

Be careful where you look

People without experience are the main target of fake job offers. If anyone asks you for money for a job, registration fees, training kits or "security deposits," walk away. Real employers pay you, not the other way around. Check the company's official website, and be careful with offers that arrive only through WhatsApp or Telegram.

A realistic timeline

I won't pretend this is instant. For most people, going from zero to a first job takes a few months of steady effort, sometimes longer in a slow market. You'll hear a lot of silence and a few rejections. That's normal and it doesn't say anything about your worth.

Rough stage What you're doing
Weeks 1 to 2 Choose a direction, look at job postings, list the skills they ask for
Weeks 3 to 6 Learn the core skills, finish a course, start a small project
Weeks 7 to 8 Finish the project, build your resume, LinkedIn and portfolio
Week 9 onwards Apply in a focused way, reach out to people, practise interviews
Ongoing Keep learning, improve based on feedback, don't stop after one rejection

The mistakes I'd skip

  • Sending the same resume to everyone without any changes
  • Waiting for the "perfect" first job instead of a good-enough one
  • Collecting certificates and never building anything
  • Taking silence personally and quitting after twenty applications
  • Being vague about what you want
  • Paying anyone for a promised job

One last thing

Having no experience feels like the biggest problem, but it's really just the starting position. Everyone who got hired for their first job had it too. What got them through was usually unglamorous: a project built over a few weekends, a polite message to a stranger, a lower-paying first role that taught them a lot. None of that needs luck. It needs a bit of patience and some stubbornness, and you can start on it today.

What kind of job are you trying to get into? Tell me in the comments and I'll suggest a first project to build.
