So Where Should Your Photo Actually Go?

LinkedIn. Genuinely, that's really it. Your LinkedIn photo matters a lot more than people realize — recruiters absolutely judge that one, and it should look current, approachable, and professional. People form an opinion about your LinkedIn photo in roughly the same few seconds they'd glance at a resume, so it's not like photos don't matter anywhere. They just belong somewhere else.

Where Photo Needed?
Resume No — leave it off
LinkedIn profile Yes, and keep it recent
Portfolio website Optional, depends on the field you're in
Modeling/acting resume (special case) Yes, that's just how that industry works
Email signature Optional, not a big deal either way

A Few Exceptions Worth Knowing

Like most advice, this isn't a universal rule carved in stone. There are a handful of situations where it genuinely doesn't apply:

  • Some countries — Germany, and parts of Asia in particular — still expect a photo on resumes, so it's worth checking local hiring norms before assuming the US/UK standard applies everywhere
  • Creative industries like acting, modeling, or certain performance-based roles genuinely require a photo as part of the application
  • If a job posting explicitly asks for a photo to be included, just follow the instruction, don't overthink it
  • Internal company transfers sometimes use a slightly different, more relaxed format where a photo doesn't matter either way

Outside of those specific cases though, my honest take is just leave it off. Your resume has exactly one job — get you an interview. Let your actual work history do that heavy lifting, not your headshot.

What To Do Instead

If you're used to having a photo on your resume and now feel like something's missing without it, here's what to fill that space with instead:

  • A short, specific summary line at the top — not a generic "hardworking professional seeking opportunities" line, but something that actually says what you do and what you're good at
  • One more quantified achievement from your most recent role
  • A skills section tailored to the actual job description you're applying for
  • Extra white space — believe it or not, a resume that's slightly less cramped actually reads easier and looks more confident

None of these feel as visually exciting as a nice headshot, sure. But they're doing actual work for you, which is more than a photo can say.

Did you have a photo on your resume before? Curious whether it ever came up in an interview, good or bad — drop it in the comments.

article_title: How to Identify Fake Job Offers and Recruitment Scams
meta_title: How to Identify Fake Job Offers and Recruitment Scams
meta_description: Got a suspicious job offer? Learn the red flags of fake job offers and recruitment scams, how to verify a company, and what to do if you’ve already been targeted.
meta_keyword: how to identify fake job offers, fake job offer signs, recruitment scam red flags, how to check if a job offer is real, job offer asking for money, fake offer letter check, whatsapp job scam, like and earn job scam, how to report job fraud in India

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
There's a boy in my building, just out of college, who was desperate for his first job like most of us were at that age. One evening he got a WhatsApp message from a "recruiter" at some big-sounding company. His resume had been shortlisted, apparently. A chat interview, an offer letter two days later, and a salary nearly double what freshers normally get. The only small thing was a refundable "security deposit" of a few thousand rupees, to block his seat. He paid it. After that the number stopped replying, the email on the offer letter bounced, and the real HR of that company told him they'd never heard of him.

He lost the money, sure. But he told me later that what hurt more was the two weeks he'd spent feeling like his life had finally started. That part you can't get refunded.

Fake job offers are everywhere now, mostly because they hit people at exactly the wrong moment, when they badly need a job and want to believe. The scammers have also improved. The logos look right, the letters look right, even the language is polished. The good news is that most of the signs are easy to see once someone points them out, so let's go through them.

If they ask for money, stop

This is the one rule I'd tattoo on every job seeker's hand. A real employer pays you. They don't charge you. Registration fee, training kit, laptop deposit, "background verification charges," refundable security money, visa processing, insurance. Different names, same scam. Companies cover their own hiring costs, and if a background check is needed, they pay for it.

There's one small grey area, which is training or placement institutes that charge for an actual course. But that's a separate, clearly stated service, not a "job offer" with a fee stuck on the front. If someone calls it an offer and wants money before you've drawn a single salary, walk away.

The smaller signs

Scams rarely depend on one trick. It's usually a pile of small things that look okay on their own and feel wrong together.

What you notice Why it bothers me
You never applied but they say you're shortlisted Could be a genuine cold message on LinkedIn, but check the profile properly before replying
The whole interview happens on WhatsApp or Telegram chat Real hiring almost always has a call or video round with a named person
The offer arrives in a day or two with hardly any questions Companies compare candidates, and that takes time
Salary is way above market for your experience It's bait. Plain and simple
Email comes from Gmail, Yahoo or Outlook HR teams use the company's own domain
Job description is vague, no real role or team Copy-pasted text, because there's no actual job behind it
"Pay today or the seat goes" Urgency is there to stop you from thinking
Spelling mistakes in the offer letter Official letters usually get proofread
Early requests for Aadhaar, PAN, bank details or OTP That info is collected after joining, through proper channels
"Work from home, earn per task" A very common scam format, more on it below

The "like and earn" trap

This one has caught plenty of educated, careful people, so don't feel clever about being immune. A message offers part-time work: like videos, rate hotels, boost reviews, finish small tasks. The first few tasks actually pay you, a small amount, and that's the hook. It builds trust. Then you're added to a group, and the next tasks supposedly need you to deposit money to unlock bigger rewards. You pay, they ask for more, and eventually both the money and the contact vanish.

The giveaway is simple. If you're paid for tasks that create no real value for any business, and then asked to put money in, it's a scam. Nobody who genuinely wants to give you work needs your money first.

Checking whether it's real

You don't have to play detective. A few minutes of checking catches most of these.

Check How
Company website Type the address yourself in the browser. Don't click the link in the message.
Email domain Should match the company's own domain. Look closely for tiny changes like an extra letter or a hyphen.
Careers page A real company hiring usually lists the role on its own site too
Recruiter's LinkedIn Look at how old the profile is, their connections and whether they actually work there. A thin, brand-new profile is a bad sign.
Address and registration Search the company name with the words "reviews" or "scam"
Employee reviews Glassdoor, AmbitionBox and similar sites. Read the recent ones.
Phone Call the number listed on the official website and ask if this recruiter and this role exist

That last one is the most reliable of all, and almost nobody does it. Two minutes on the phone with the real HR department can save you a lot of trouble.

What normal looks like

It's easier to spot strange things when you know the usual pattern. You apply (or you're contacted on a verified platform), there's a screening call, then one or more interviews with people who have names, maybe a test or assignment, and then an offer from an official email address. Your ID documents are collected after you accept, through the company's own system. And at no point do you pay anything.

Some small companies do move fast, and that's fine. But fast shouldn't mean no interview, no named interviewer and a request for money.

Be stingy with your documents

Even if you never pay a rupee, scammers can still hurt you through what you share. Don't send Aadhaar, PAN, passport or bank details until you've confirmed the company is real. Never share an OTP, not for any job, not ever. Don't send photos of ID cards to a stranger either, since those get used to open accounts and take loans. And your UPI PIN or card details are never needed to get paid. If anyone asks for them, that's the end of the conversation.

Where these things turn up

Pretty much everywhere job seekers are. WhatsApp and Telegram, SMS, spam email, social media ads, fake websites copying real company pages. Even real job portals aren't fully safe, since fake listings occasionally get posted there, and some scammers contact people who've uploaded resumes. So being on a portal doesn't prove anything. Run the same checks.

Jobs abroad need extra care

I'm giving these their own section because the money involved is usually much bigger. A fake overseas offer promises a great salary in the Gulf or Europe, then asks for visa fees, agent fees, flight charges. Some even send visa copies that look very convincing. Make sure the recruitment agency is registered with the proper government authority, don't pay large sums in cash, get everything in writing, and verify the foreign employer separately. If you can't verify the company, think very hard before paying anyone.

If you think you've been caught

Where you are What to do
Suspicious message, but you haven't paid Stop replying, don't click links, block the number and report it on the platform
You shared documents or details Note exactly what you shared, watch your accounts and think about telling your bank
You already paid Call your bank or payment app right away and report the fraud. Speed really matters here
You want to report it In India, use the cybercrime reporting portal (cybercrime.gov.in) or call 1930, and report the profile or listing on the platform too
You lost money and feel embarrassed Don't. Clever people get caught, and reporting early gives the best chance of tracing it

Save everything before you report: screenshots, chats, receipts, emails, phone numbers. Scammers often delete their side later.

Before you trust any offer

  • Nobody has asked me for money, not even a "refundable" amount
  • I checked the company on its official site, not through a link in the message
  • The email is from the company's own domain
  • I spoke to a real person and confirmed they work there
  • The salary and the speed of the offer are believable
  • I haven't shared OTPs, PINs or ID documents too early

The simplest rule I know

If something feels off, it usually is. Your gut is a decent early-warning system, so slow down and check. A real opportunity doesn't vanish within an hour, and a company that genuinely wants you will wait while you verify. A scammer, on the other hand, will push harder, and that's honestly the clearest sign you'll ever get.

Have you or someone you know ever received a fake job offer? Tell me what gave it away in the comments, it might stop someone else from falling for the same trick.

article_title: Best Resume for Different Jobs: Format, Length and Style for Every Role
meta_title: Best Resume for Different Jobs: Format and Tips
meta_description: Find the best resume for your job type. Format, length and style tips for freshers, IT, sales, finance, teaching, healthcare, design, government jobs and more.
meta_keyword: best resume for different jobs, best resume format, resume for different job types, resume format for freshers, resume for IT jobs, resume for sales jobs, resume for finance jobs, government job resume, resume for career change, chronological vs functional vs hybrid resume

category.article_description: Expert tips and useful guidance to help you create a professional, ATS-friendly resume and improve your chances of getting hired.

contents.content:
There is no single resume that works for every job. A plain, one-column resume suits a bank. A designer can get away with more style. A government application may need a fixed format that looks nothing like either. People who send the same file everywhere are mostly guessing.

This guide first explains the three basic formats, then goes through the common job types one by one: what to put on top, how long it should be, and what to leave out.

The three basic resume formats

Almost every resume is one of three layouts. Fancy design is just decoration on top.

Format How it works Good for Less suitable when
Reverse chronological Newest job first, going back A steady career in one field You have big gaps or are changing fields completely
Functional Skills first, work history cut to a few lines Freshers, career changers, people returning after a break The company uses strict screening software, since some systems read this layout badly
Hybrid A skills summary on top, then history in order People with mixed experience You have almost nothing to list yet

When you are not sure, use reverse chronological. Recruiters know where to look in it, and screening software reads it well. The other two are for particular situations.

What every resume needs

Whatever the job, a few things stay the same. Use an email address that looks serious. Stick to one clean font. Write a two or three line summary that says what you do. "Hardworking professional looking for a challenging role" is on thousands of resumes, so it tells the reader nothing. Save the file as a PDF unless the company asks for something else, and name it properly. Rahul_Sharma_Resume.pdf is good. resume_final_new_v3 (2).pdf is not.

Proofread it, then read it out loud once. Your mouth will stumble on mistakes your eyes skipped.

How plain or creative should it look?

The more formal the industry, the plainer the resume should be. Creative fields can take more style, but readability still comes first.

One exception to the scale: IT sits in the middle for design but at the plain end for layout. Many tech companies run resumes through screening software first, so a clean single column is safer than a clever one.

Freshers and fresh graduates

With no job history, your resume will feel thin, and that is normal. Employers hiring freshers already know you lack experience. They want signs that you can learn and that you have done something beyond attending lectures.

Section What to put
Length One page
Top Name, contact details and a short objective written for this role
Education Near the top: degree, college, year, and CGPA if it is decent
Projects Two to four, each with a line on what you built and what you learned
Internships Even a one-month internship counts. Say what came out of it
Skills Only skills you can talk about in an interview
Extras Certificates, clubs, volunteering, competitions

The usual fresher mistake is listing every school prize and ten skills they have used once. Choose the best few and cut the rest.

IT and software jobs

Tech recruiters mostly want to know what you can build and with which tools. Since many companies filter resumes with software first, this is a field where heavy formatting can cost you. Use one column, no graphics and no text boxes.

Group skills by type (languages, frameworks, databases, cloud) instead of one long comma list. Put a GitHub or live project link where it is easy to see. Write bullets like "reduced API response time by 35%" instead of "worked on APIs". Copy technology names from the job description exactly, because the software matches words and not meanings. Skip skill bars that say you are 80% good at Python. Nobody knows what that means.

One page works for under five years of experience. After that, two pages are fine.

Marketing, digital marketing and content

These resumes can show a bit more personality, but numbers still carry the weight: traffic growth, leads, conversion rates, ad spend and what it returned. If you ran a campaign and cannot remember the figures, check old reports. It is worth the effort.

List your tools (Google Analytics, Meta Ads, SEMrush, HubSpot, Canva) and link to a portfolio, blog or campaign samples. A slightly modern layout is fine, as long as it stays readable.

Sales and business development

Sales is one of the most number-driven fields. A sales resume without figures looks weak next to one with them, even when the first person is the better seller.

Weak line Stronger line (example numbers)
Responsible for sales in my region Achieved 118% of annual target across a three-state region
Handled client relationships Kept 92% of key accounts for two years in a row
Did cold calling and follow-ups Generated around 45 qualified leads a month, about a fifth of which became paying clients

The figures above are examples to show the style. Use your own real numbers. Put targets, revenue and rankings where the eye lands first. One or two pages is enough.

Finance, accounting and banking

This is a conservative field. Black text on white, simple headings and reverse chronological order is the safe choice. Fancy design tends to work against you.

List the software you know, such as Tally, SAP, QuickBooks or Power BI, and the Excel functions you use (pivot tables, VLOOKUP, macros). Put certifications like CA, CFA or CMA near the top. Give figures where you can, for example the value of accounts you handled or how much you shortened the month-end closing. Check for typos twice. In a job built on accuracy, one typo makes the reader wonder what else was missed.

Teaching and education

Schools and colleges look at qualifications and subject knowledge first. Lead with your degree, B.Ed, and TET, CTET or NET if you have them. Then list the subjects and classes you have taught and the board (CBSE, ICSE or state). If your students' results improved, say so. If you have used smart classrooms or online teaching tools, add that too, because many institutes ask about it.

Healthcare and nursing

Hospitals need to verify details, so make that easy. Put your registration or licence information, degree and certifications first. Then list the areas you have worked in (ICU, OT, paediatrics, emergency) and the type of hospital. Mention training such as BLS or ACLS and any equipment you are trained to use. Keep the layout plain and formal.

Design and creative jobs

This is the field where you can bend the rules, as long as you have the taste to do it well. A messy creative resume is worse than a boring one.

Your portfolio link matters more than the resume, so make it impossible to miss. List tools like Figma, Photoshop, Illustrator or After Effects, and name clients or brands where you can. Keep a plain, ATS-friendly version ready as well. Some companies will filter applications through software no matter how good your portfolio is.

Government jobs

Government applications work differently. There is less personal branding and more paperwork. If the notification gives a format, follow it exactly, even if it looks plain. Give full personal details when asked, such as date of birth, category and address, along with education details: board or university, year and marks.

These details are usually checked against your documents, so what you write must match your certificates exactly. A small mismatch can create real trouble later.

BPO, customer support and call centre jobs

These roles hire in large numbers, so the reader goes through resumes fast. One clean page is enough. Put your languages up front, add your typing speed if it is good, and mention any customer-facing work, including retail or part-time jobs. List the tools you have used (mostly CRM software), your shift flexibility, and numbers like satisfaction scores or calls handled per day if you have them.

Engineering and manufacturing

List the machines, software and standards you know. Then show results: less downtime, lower costs, better output, a clean safety record. Certifications such as AutoCAD, SolidWorks or Six Sigma can go in their own short section. Keep the layout plain.

HR and recruitment

Show hiring numbers like positions filled, time to hire and retention. Mention the applicant tracking tools and job portals you have used, and any onboarding or employee engagement work. Your own resume will be judged closely by people in the same field, so the formatting needs to be clean and consistent.

Career changers

If you are moving to a new field, the hybrid or functional format often helps, because skills sit above job titles. Start with a short summary that says what you are moving into and why you fit. Then group the skills that carry over, and list your past jobs after that. Add any course, certificate or side project that shows you are serious.

Do not apologise for the switch anywhere on the page. State it plainly and let the skills make the case.

Senior and leadership roles

Two pages is fine here. Open with a short executive summary that shows scale: team size, budget, business impact. Then talk about outcomes and decisions, not daily tasks. Older roles can shrink to a line or two. Nobody needs the details of your first job from eighteen years ago.

Quick comparison

Job type Best format Design Length Highlight
Fresher Hybrid or functional Simple, clean 1 page Projects, education, skills
IT / software Reverse chronological Plain, ATS-friendly 1 to 2 pages Tech stack, projects, impact
Marketing Reverse chronological Modern but readable 1 to 2 pages Metrics, tools, portfolio
Sales Reverse chronological Clean, results first 1 to 2 pages Targets, revenue
Finance / banking Reverse chronological Minimal, conservative 1 to 2 pages Certifications, software, accuracy
Teaching Reverse chronological Structured, professional 1 to 2 pages Qualifications, subjects, results
Healthcare Reverse chronological Clean, formal 1 to 2 pages Licence, clinical experience
Design / creative Hybrid Creative but tasteful 1 to 2 pages Portfolio, tools
Government As per notification Plain, document style As required Complete, matching details
BPO / support Simple chronological Easy to scan 1 page Languages, communication, CRM
Career changer Functional or hybrid Skill-focused 1 to 2 pages Transferable skills
Senior / leadership Reverse chronological Polished, minimal 2 pages Strategic impact, scale

Mistakes to avoid

  • Sending the same resume to every job
  • An email address like coolboy_2003@something
  • A photo, religion or marital status when the job did not ask for them
  • Listing duties instead of what changed because of your work
  • Crowding the page, or using a style that does not suit the industry
  • Ignoring keywords that appear in the job description
  • Exaggerating. It usually comes out at the interview or the background check.

How to put it together

Tweak the result a little for each application. Ten extra minutes per job is usually enough to move the right things to the top.

Frequently asked questions

Which resume format is best for freshers?

A hybrid or simple chronological format with education, projects and skills near the top. Keep it to one page.

Is a functional resume a bad idea?

Not always. It helps freshers and career changers, but some recruiters distrust it because it can hide gaps, and some screening software reads it badly. A hybrid format usually gives the same benefit with fewer risks.

Should I add a photo?

Not unless the job asks for one. In most cases it adds nothing, and some employers prefer resumes without photos.

How long should a resume be?

One page for freshers and for up to roughly seven or eight years of experience. Two pages for longer careers or senior roles. Do not stretch to a second page for a few lines.

Do I need a different resume for each job type?

You do not need a new one from scratch. Keep one main version and adjust the order, the summary and the skills for each type of role.

To sum up

A good resume is not about clever words or fancy design. It shows the right reader, in the way they expect to see it, that you can do this particular job. The same experience can look average or strong depending on how it is arranged, so choose the format that suits the industry and the person reading it.

article_title: Salary Negotiation: What to Say When You Get a Job Offer
meta_title: Salary Negotiation: How to Ask for More (Scripts)
meta_description: Don’t accept the first offer without a second thought. Learn what to research, what to say, how much to ask for and when it is fine not to negotiate.
meta_keyword: salary negotiation, how to negotiate salary, ask for higher salary, negotiate job offer, salary negotiation script, salary negotiation example, salary negotiation for freshers, CTC negotiation India, what to say when HR asks about salary, negotiate joining bonus

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
When a company makes you an offer, there is usually a short moment where they mention the number and wait to see what you say. A lot of people say "okay, that's fine" because they have no idea what else to say. Later they find out the number could have been a little higher if they had asked.

Negotiating does not need to be aggressive or awkward. It needs a bit of research and one or two sentences you have already thought about. This guide covers both, along with how much to ask for, what else you can negotiate apart from the base pay, and the cases where it is fine not to negotiate at all.

Is it okay to negotiate at all?

In most private companies, yes. When HR makes an offer, they usually have a range in mind for the role, not one fixed number. The first figure they say is often somewhere in the lower or middle part of that range. That is just how budgets work. It does not mean they are trying to cheat you.

There are exceptions. Government jobs and many campus placements have fixed pay scales. Some internships and very junior roles also have a standard package for everyone. In those cases there is nothing to negotiate, and asking can sound strange. Outside of those, a polite question is normal and most hiring managers expect it.

Do your research first

Walking in with real numbers changes the whole conversation. You are no longer saying "please give me more". You are saying "this is what the role usually pays, and this is where I fit".

  • Look up the exact role and city. A sales executive in a metro city and one in a smaller town can have very different pay.
  • Compare two or three similar companies. Sites like Glassdoor, AmbitionBox and LinkedIn salary insights give a rough idea. Treat the numbers as a guide, since they come from self-reported data and can be old.
  • List what you bring. Years of experience, tools you know well, certificates, and a competing offer if you really have one.
  • Decide your minimum before the call. Do it quietly at home, so you are not working it out under pressure while someone waits on the line.
  • Understand the structure. In India, offers are often given as CTC. Find out how much is fixed, how much is variable, and what your monthly in-hand pay will be after deductions. Two offers with the same CTC can feel very different at the end of the month.

What to actually say

You do not need a speech. A short, calm version works better than a long one.

"Thank you for the offer. I am excited about this role. Based on my research and the responsibilities we discussed, I was hoping for something closer to [number]. Is there any flexibility on that?"

It does three things. It says thanks, it gives a reason, and it asks one clear question. Many people leave out the reason, which makes the request sound random. Others apologise so much that it sounds like they do not believe in their own number. Keep it steady and stop talking after the question. A pause is fine.

If they ask for your current salary

This question comes up often in India. You can answer with what you are looking for instead, for example "I am looking for something in the range of X to Y for this role". If you do share your current pay, tell the truth. Companies can check through payslips, bank statements or Form 16, and a lie can cost you the job even after you have joined.

How much should you ask for?

There is no single right number. The table below is a rough guide, and it changes with the industry, the city and how much the company needs the role filled.

Situation Approach
First job, no experience Ask for a small increase, maybe 5 to 10 percent, or none if the package is fixed. Learning, mentoring and a clear role often matter more at this stage.
Changing jobs with 2 to 4 years of experience Use your current pay and market data together. A jump of 15 to 25 percent is a common target in many fields, but it depends on the industry.
You have another offer Mention it plainly and without threats. For example: "I have another offer at X, but I would prefer to join here if we can get closer to that number."
Raise or promotion at your current company Bring proof of what you have done and the extra work you took on. Years in the company alone are a weak reason.

Asking for 10 to 12 percent more with a clear reason is received very differently from asking for 40 percent more with nothing behind it. The first looks like a normal conversation. The second looks like a guess.

It is not only the base number

If the company says the base pay cannot move, there may still be other things you can ask about. Depending on the company, these can include a joining bonus, work from home days, an earlier salary review, a learning budget, a different designation, or a better split between fixed and variable pay. A formal review after six months instead of twelve is something many companies agree to more easily than a higher base.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Saying yes on the call before you have seen the offer in writing
  • Making up a current salary or a competing offer that does not exist
  • Giving ultimatums like "give me this or I walk"
  • Asking for a big number without any reason behind it
  • Bringing up salary in the first round, before the company has shown interest in you
  • Focusing only on the base pay and ignoring variable pay, notice period terms and probation rules
  • Trying to negotiate after you have already signed

When it is fine to accept the first number

You do not have to negotiate every time. If the offer already matches or beats what your research showed, accept it with a clear conscience. The same goes for fixed-pay roles, entry-level internships, or situations where you need to join quickly and a few extra percent is not worth the delay. Negotiation is a tool to use when it makes sense. It is not a duty.

After you agree

Ask for the final terms in the offer letter and read it properly before signing. Check that the CTC breakup, joining date, notice period, probation period and variable pay match what was discussed. If anything was agreed on a call, such as an early review or a joining bonus, make sure it is written down. Verbal promises are easy to forget later.

Frequently asked questions

Can a company withdraw an offer if I negotiate?

It is rare when you are polite and your request is reasonable. It is not impossible, though, and there is no guarantee. This is another reason to avoid ultimatums and to know your own minimum before you start.

Should I negotiate over the phone or by email?

Either works. A phone call lets you hear their tone and respond quickly. Email gives you time to think and leaves a written record. Many people discuss it on a call and then confirm the final numbers by email.

Can a fresher negotiate?

Yes, if the company does not have a fixed package for freshers. Keep the ask small and give a reason, such as a relevant internship, a project or a skill the role needs. If the pay is fixed, ask about learning opportunities or an early review instead.

What if they say no?

Stay polite and ask whether anything else can be adjusted, like a review date or work from home. Then decide if the offer works for you as it is. Staying calm leaves the door open for future roles at the same company.

Should I mention another offer if I do not have one?

No. It is dishonest, and if the company asks for details you will have nothing to show. Use market research and your own skills as your reasons instead.

To sum up

Good salary talks rarely involve a fight. Find out what the role normally pays, know your minimum, ask one clear question with a reason behind it, and get the final terms in writing. If the first offer is already fair, take it and move on.

contents.content:
Nobody reads your resume the way you wrote it. You spent hours on it. The recruiter gives it a few seconds, maybe ten, then decides yes, no or maybe. When fifty people have applied for one job, that is just how it goes.

So the whole game is making those few seconds count. Put the useful stuff where the eye lands first, cut the rest, and keep it easy to scan. This post goes through the resume section by section and tells you what I would keep and what I would drop.

Which format?

Use reverse-chronological, where your latest job comes first. It is the one HR people expect, and it is the one the screening software reads best. There is not much reason to try anything else.

A fresher has no jobs to list, so start with education, internships and projects instead. And if you are moving to a different field, you can open with a short skills block before the job list. That is about the only case for bending the format.

The top of the page

Name, phone number, email, city. Add your LinkedIn link only if the profile is filled in properly. An empty LinkedIn page does more harm than leaving the link out.

Check the email address. Something built from your own name is fine. A nickname from school days is not. You can skip your full postal address, your photo, your date of birth and your marital status. Some Indian companies still ask for these on their own forms, and in that case give them, but there is no need to put them on every resume by default.

The summary

This is the two or three lines under your name. Most people fill it with words like "hardworking" and "passionate", which tells the reader nothing. What helps is the plain fact of what you do and how long you have done it.

Doesn't say much Says something
Motivated fresher looking to learn and grow with a reputed organisation. BCom 2024. Six-month internship in accounts payable at a CA firm, Tally Prime course done. Looking for a junior accounts job.
Dedicated professional with good communication skills. Retail supervisor, five years in clothing stores. Runs a team of four, deals with customer complaints, sends the daily sales report.

The left column could be on anyone's resume. That is the problem with it.

Work experience

This is the part people read most closely, so spend most of your time here. For every job, write the title, the company, the city and the dates. Under that, three to five lines about what you actually did.

Start each line with a verb. "Handled billing and cash counting" is better than "Was responsible for billing and cash counting". It is shorter and it sounds like you did something. Try not to start four lines in a row with the same word, because it starts to look like a template.

Then, if you can, say what came out of it. Not every line will have a result, and that is fine. But the lines that do will stand out from the rest.

Numbers

Anything you can count, count it. How many people were in your team, how many customers you saw in a day, how much the sales went up, how many hours a week you saved. "Handled customer queries" could mean five a day or five hundred. "Handled 30 to 40 queries a day" tells the reader exactly what your job looked like.

If you do not remember the exact figure, give your best estimate and write "around" in front of it. Do not invent anything. In an interview someone will ask how you got that number, and you should be able to answer.

Skills

Open the job posting next to your resume. Whatever tools and skills it keeps repeating, and you really have, put them in your skills section using the same words. If the posting says "MS Excel", write "MS Excel". A lot of screening software matches exact words, so "spreadsheet knowledge" may not count.

Leave out "team player", "hardworking" and "quick learner". Everyone writes them. And skip the little rating bars. Nobody can tell what 70% in communication is supposed to mean.

Education, certificates, projects

Degree, college, year. Add marks or CGPA when they are good, or when the company asks for them. After you have a couple of years of work behind you, education can drop to the bottom and take up one line.

Freshers should put projects and internships to work here. Treat them like jobs. Say what the project was, what part you did and what tools you used. A certificate is worth listing when it connects to the job, and not worth much when it does not.

ATS, in plain words

Many companies, especially bigger ones, run every resume through software called an applicant tracking system, or ATS, before a human opens it. The software pulls the text out and sorts it into boxes. A fancy layout can throw it off, so your work history ends up in the wrong place or goes missing.

To avoid that, keep to one column, use ordinary headings like Work Experience and Education, and stay away from tables and text boxes for anything important. Do not put your phone number in the page header or footer, as some systems skip that area. Stick with fonts like Arial, Calibri or Times New Roman. As for file type, do what the portal asks. If it does not say, a PDF is usually safe.

Looks and length

Pick one or two fonts and keep the text between 10 and 12 points. Leave decent margins. Write every date in the same style and keep the gaps between sections even. Uneven spacing is one of those things readers notice without knowing why the page feels messy.

One page is enough until you have seven or eight years of experience. After that two pages are fine. What you should avoid is a second page with just three lines on it. Trim a little and pull it back to one.

Change it for each job

Sending the exact same file to every company is the easy way, and it shows. You do not have to rewrite everything. Just read the posting, pick the three or four things it cares about most, and make sure those are near the top of your resume. Reorder a few bullets, tweak the summary, update the skills. Ten minutes is enough.

Mistakes I see again and again

  • Listing duties ("responsible for stock") and no results
  • Keeping a job from twelve years ago that has nothing to do with the role
  • An old phone number or email still sitting at the top
  • Mixing past and present tense in the same job
  • A file named resume_final_final2.pdf. Call it Firstname_Lastname_Resume.pdf.
  • "References available on request". Everyone knows. Delete it.

Read it out loud

After a few hours of editing you stop seeing the page. The eyes just slide over mistakes. Reading it aloud, slowly, makes you catch the missing words and the clumsy lines. Then check the phone number and email one character at a time, because a typo there means no one can reach you. And ask a friend to read it. Another person will find something in two minutes that you missed in two hours.

Before you hit send
  • Phone and email are right
  • Summary says what you do
  • Bullets start with a verb and show a result where possible
  • Skills match the posting
  • One column, same fonts, same date style
  • Spelling checked, file named properly

Questions people ask

Do I need a career objective?

Mostly no. A summary that says what you do is more useful. If you are a fresher, one line naming the exact role you want is okay.

What about a gap in my work history?

A few months does not need an explanation. For a longer gap, one line is enough, like "Career break, family reasons" or "Preparing for government exams". If you did a course or some freelance work in that time, add it.

PDF or Word?

Follow the portal. If it gives no instruction, send a PDF, since the layout will not change on someone else's phone. A few older systems read Word better, so it is worth a quick look at what the company asks for.

How far back should I go?

Ten to fifteen years is plenty for most jobs. Older ones can shrink to a title and company name.

Is it okay to use a template?

Yes, if it is a simple one-column design. A template like the free ones on ResumeSathi takes care of the layout so you can spend your time on the writing. It cannot fix weak bullet points, though. That part is on you.

To sum up

You do not need a clever design. You need a page that shows quickly what you have done and what you can do. Lead with the useful things, add real numbers, keep the layout plain, and read it once more before sending.

article_title: How to Resign From a Job Properly: Steps, Letter Samples and Checklist
meta_title: How to Resign From a Job: Steps, Letter, Checklist
meta_description: How to resign the right way: what to check first, how to tell your manager, a sample letter, notice period tips and a last-day checklist.
meta_keyword: how to resign from a job, resignation letter sample, how to write a resignation letter, how to tell your boss you are quitting, notice period buyout, resignation letter for new job, exit interview tips, last day checklist, relieving letter, full and final settlement

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
Handing in a resignation takes five minutes. Getting out cleanly takes a bit longer than that.

The letter is the easy part. The trouble starts later. You find out the notice period is 90 days and not 30. The relieving letter doesn't turn up for weeks. Your manager, who was friendly last month, goes cold when the new company calls for a reference. Almost all of this can be avoided if you do a few things in the right order, so that's what this post is about. It's general information, not legal advice, and your own appointment letter has the final say on the rules.

Get the new offer in writing first

Don't resign on the basis of a phone call. "We'll send the letter next week" means nothing until the letter is in your inbox. Offers get delayed. Background checks drag on. Now and then the role just disappears. If you've already resigned by then, you're stuck, with no leverage and a manager who now knows you're leaving.

Then read your appointment letter

All of it, including the boring clauses. You're looking for the notice period, whether a buyout is allowed, any service bond, any joining bonus you'd have to pay back, and a non-compete if there is one. Better to find a surprise now than in your last week.

Tell your manager first

Not HR, not your work friends. Your manager. In person or on a call, if you can.

"I wanted you to hear this from me first. I've decided to move on and I'll send in my resignation today. I'll make sure my work is handed over properly."

You don't need a long explanation. "I got an opportunity I want to take" is plenty. And this isn't the moment for a list of complaints. It won't change anything, and it's exactly what your manager will remember when somebody asks about you a year from now.

The letter

Short. That's the main thing. Your designation, your last working day, one polite line. You don't have to name the new company or give a reason.

Subject: Resignation – [Your Name], [Designation]

Dear [Manager's name],

I'm resigning from my role as [designation]. My last day will be [date], which is when my [60-day] notice period ends.

I'll finish whatever is pending and write up a handover for the person who takes over. If HR needs anything else from me, just tell me.

Thank you for the time here. I learned a lot working with this team.

Regards,
[Your Name]
[Employee ID]

If the new company needs you earlier than your notice allows, put a line in the letter asking for it. Something like: "Because of my joining date at the new organisation, could my last working day be [date]? I'll complete the handover in that time and stay reachable afterwards. If it isn't possible, I understand." Don't make it sound like a demand.

Serve it, shorten it, or pay it off

Those are the three ways a notice period usually goes. Most people simply work through it. Some ask for early release, which is a request, so the company can say no. And some contracts allow a buyout, where you pay the company for the days you skip. Look at what yours says before you decide anything.

Whatever gets agreed, get it in writing. Even a two-line email will do. Verbal promises have a way of vanishing when the final settlement is being calculated.

If they make a counter-offer

It happens. Suddenly you're worth more money and a better title. Before you say yes, ask yourself why you wanted to leave in the first place. If the answer is pay, fine, maybe that fixes it. If the answer is the work, the manager, or no growth, then a bigger number won't change any of that, and you'll probably be back in the same spot in a year. Decide this before the conversation. It's harder to think clearly when your boss is sitting across from you asking you to stay.

Handover, even if you're annoyed

People forget most of what you did at work. They remember how you left.

So write the handover down. Open tasks, where the files are, who the contacts are, what's pending, what deadlines are coming. Then walk someone through it. If part of your work is tricky, record a short screen video, because that saves the team more trouble than any document.

One warning. Don't copy customer data, internal documents or code to your personal email or drive, however harmless it feels. Companies take that seriously and it can turn into a legal problem. Take your own contacts and your own certificates, and leave the rest.

If HR asks for an exit interview, be honest, but keep it calm. Real problems, like unclear targets or no training, are worth mentioning with an example. Personal attacks aren't. These notes go into a file, and files get passed around.

Your last day

Here's what to leave with, and what to hand back.

The full and final settlement (F&F) is your last salary plus any leave encashment and other dues, minus any deductions. Companies take different amounts of time to clear it. Ask HR for a date and keep their reply. Gratuity usually needs a certain number of years of continuous service, commonly five, but the rules vary in some cases, so confirm with HR and don't assume.

If the relieving letter is late and nobody gives you a reason, even though you served your notice and handed over, write to HR asking for a date. If that doesn't work, go to a senior HR person. Think about legal advice only if it keeps dragging on.

A couple of quick questions

Can you resign by email? Yes, most companies accept it. Send it to your manager and HR together and keep a copy. Can you take leave during notice? Depends on the company. Some don't allow it and some extend the notice by the days you take, so ask first.

And should you resign before you have another job? Usually no. The exception is when the job is hurting your health. Then look at your savings, plan the gap, and go.

That's about it. Don't badmouth the company online after you leave either. It's tempting, and it never helps.

contents.content:
So you're staring at a blank resume template again, and somehow it still feels confusing. I get it. There are literally hundreds of resume designs floating around online right now, and half of them look like they were made for a graphic designer's portfolio, not for someone applying to an actual job. Some have sidebars, some have circular skill meters, some have photos and colored headers that take up a third of the page. And then there's the plain kind — just black text, a name at the top, a few clean sections, nothing flashy. People often assume the fancier one wins. In real hiring situations, that's usually not true.

Before picking a template, it actually helps to step back and understand that resumes aren't just "designs." They fall into a few real categories, and each one is built around a different hiring situation. Once you know which bucket you're in, choosing a layout becomes a lot less stressful.

The Four Resume Types Nobody Really Explains Properly

Most career sites throw templates at you without explaining why they exist. Here's the short version, without the jargon.

  • Chronological Resume — This is the old faithful. Work history listed newest to oldest. Recruiters are trained to scan this format fast because it's what they've seen a thousand times. If your career has been fairly linear, this is almost always the safest bet.
  • Functional Resume — Built around skills instead of a strict timeline. Good if you've had gaps, took a break, or you're switching into a completely different field and don't want your past job titles to be the first thing someone judges you on.
  • Combination Resume — A blend of both. You get a skills section up top and then a chronological work history below it. This tends to suit people with a handful of years of experience who want to highlight both.
  • Creative or Visual Resume — Heavy on design, color, icons, sometimes even illustrations. Common in design, advertising, or media roles where the resume itself is expected to show off some visual sense.

None of these is "the best" one objectively. It really depends on what job you're applying for and who's going to be reading it — a human, a hiring software, or both.

Where a Plain, No-Nonsense Layout Actually Fits

Now, the layout style we're talking about here — bold name up top, one horizontal line for email, phone, city, and website, then clean sections for Summary, Skills, Experience, and Education stacked one after another — this is basically a stripped-down chronological resume. No sidebars. No color blocks fighting for attention. No decorative graphics pretending to be relevant. Just information, laid out in the order someone would naturally want to read it.

There's a reason this style keeps showing up again and again, even though it looks "boring" compared to some templates. A huge number of companies now run resumes through Applicant Tracking Systems before a human even glances at them. These systems are notoriously bad at reading resumes with tables, multiple columns, or graphics — sometimes they scramble the text order completely or skip sections entirely. A single-column, text-first resume almost never has that problem. It just gets read the way it's meant to be read.

So while a creative resume might turn heads visually, a simple layout like this one is often the one that actually survives the first digital filter and lands in front of an actual person, which honestly matters a lot more than how it looks on a screen.

Who This Layout Actually Makes Sense For

This kind of clean, no-frills format tends to work particularly well for:

  • Retail, sales, and customer-facing roles, where clarity and quick scanning matter more than visual impression
  • Cashier, POS operator, and front-desk type positions
  • Fresh graduates or first-time job seekers who don't have a long history to fill up space with anyway
  • Operational roles — warehouse, inventory, logistics assistant positions
  • Any application submitted online through a company portal, since most of those run ATS scanning
  • People switching careers who still want something that reads clean and doesn't distract from the actual content

On the flip side, if you're applying somewhere design-heavy — say, a branding studio, a UI/UX role, or something in the creative arts — a plain layout might actually undersell you a little. In those fields, a bit of visual flair is almost part of the job requirement, since the resume is a small sample of your design sense. But for retail, sales, admin, operations, and most entry-level corporate jobs, keeping it simple usually works in your favor rather than against it.

Small Details That Make This Kind of Layout Work

What's interesting is that even a "simple" resume has small design decisions baked into it that make it easier to read. A few worth noticing:

  • The name is large and bold, so it's the very first thing anyone's eyes land on — which is exactly how it should be.
  • Contact details are squeezed into one single line instead of stacking on separate lines, which saves vertical space that can be used elsewhere.
  • Section headers are separated with a thin horizontal rule rather than a colored background, which keeps things visually calm without wasting ink or looking cluttered.
  • Skill levels are shown with small tags like Intermediate, Advanced, or Master instead of long-winded explanations, so a recruiter gets the picture in half a second.
  • Each section has a clear beginning and end, so someone skimming for ten seconds — which is genuinely how long most resumes get looked at — can still find what they need without hunting for it.

None of these choices are accidental, even though the layout looks effortless. Good simple design usually takes more thought than a busy one — it's the difference between removing everything unnecessary and never thinking about what was necessary in the first place.

Why People Still Underestimate Simple Resumes

There's a weird bias people carry when they're job hunting — they think a resume needs to "look impressive" the way a poster or an invitation card does. But a resume isn't marketing material in that sense. It's closer to a form that needs to be filled out clearly so a stranger, who has thirty other resumes to get through that same hour, can quickly figure out whether you're worth calling. Every unnecessary design element is basically friction. It slows the reader down, even by a second or two, and in a stack of applications, seconds matter more than people realize.

This doesn't mean every resume should look identical or lifeless. A little personality in the wording, a well-chosen accent color, a clean font — all of that is fine and can still make a resume feel put-together. The line is between "designed with intent" and "designed to look busy." The layout we've been talking about sits comfortably on the right side of that line.

A Small Reality Check

Here's the thing nobody likes to hear: the layout is just the container. It genuinely does not matter how clean, minimal, or well-organized a resume looks if the content inside it is vague, exaggerated, or copied word-for-word from a template example. Recruiters read hundreds of resumes and they can tell within seconds when something feels generic. Numbers should be real. Skills should reflect what you can actually do. Job descriptions should sound like they came from your own experience, not from a list of buzzwords someone else wrote.

A well-structured layout can absolutely help someone get noticed faster and get past automated filters. But at the end of the day, it's the honesty and specificity of what's written inside that gets someone an interview call. The format just makes sure that message actually reaches someone in the first place, instead of getting lost or misread before it ever gets a fair chance.

article_title: Skills vs Degree: What Matters More for Getting a Job?

meta_description: Skills or a degree — which one actually gets you hired? A practical, field-by-field breakdown to help you figure out where to invest your time.

contents.content:
Somebody asked me this the other day, half joking — "should I just drop out and learn to code instead?" I didn't have a one-line answer for them, and honestly, nobody really does. The truth sits somewhere in between, and it depends a lot more on the industry, the role, and the actual person than most advice online admits.

Still, it's worth pulling apart properly, because this question isn't going away. If anything, it's coming up more often now that self-taught developers, bootcamp grads, and certificate-holders are landing roles that used to require a specific degree on paper.

Why This Debate Even Exists

A degree used to be the default filter. No degree, no interview — that was pretty much it for a long time. But a few things have shifted that:

  • Tech and creative fields grew fast enough that formal education couldn't keep up with what the job actually required
  • Free and low-cost learning resources made it possible to build real skills outside a classroom
  • Portfolios, GitHub profiles, and project work started speaking louder than a transcript in a lot of hiring conversations
  • Some companies quietly removed degree requirements from job postings, especially for technical roles

That said, this shift hasn't touched every industry equally, which is really the whole point of this post.

Where Skills Tend to Win

In some fields, what you can actually do outweighs what your certificate says, and it's not close.

Field Why Skills Matter More Here
Software Development Employers usually just want to see working code, a portfolio, or GitHub activity
Digital Marketing Results from past campaigns say more than a marketing degree ever could
Graphic / UI Design A strong portfolio does the talking, formal design education is a bonus at best
Freelancing / Content Creation Clients care about output and reliability, not where you studied
Sales Track record and communication ability matter far more than qualifications on paper

Where a Degree Still Carries Real Weight

On the flip side, there are fields where skipping a degree basically closes the door before you even apply.

Field Why the Degree Still Matters
Medicine Legally required, no shortcut exists here regardless of skill level
Law Licensing and bar exams are tied directly to formal education
Government Jobs Eligibility criteria are usually degree-based by default
Core Engineering (Civil, Mechanical) Safety-critical work often requires certified, degree-backed knowledge
Academic / Research Roles Degrees are essentially the entry ticket, sometimes multiple of them

What Recruiters Are Actually Looking At

I've heard enough hiring managers talk about this to notice a pattern — most of them aren't choosing one over the other, they're weighing both against the role in front of them.

Hiring Factor What It Signals
Relevant Skills Can this person do the job on day one, or close to it
Degree Baseline discipline, foundational knowledge, sometimes just a filtering tool for large applicant pools
Portfolio / Past Work Proof over promises, this often overrides both of the above
Certifications A middle ground — shows initiative without needing four years
Interview Performance Can override a weak resume on either side entirely

So What Should You Actually Do?

This isn't really a "pick one" situation, no matter how the question gets framed online. A few honest points worth considering:

  • If you're aiming for a licensed profession, there's no getting around the degree, plan around that reality
  • If you're going into a skill-driven field, put your energy into building something you can actually show, not just certificates you can list
  • A degree plus strong skills will almost always beat either one alone, this isn't an either-or as often as people think
  • If you already have a degree in an unrelated field, don't assume it's wasted, transferable skills count more than people give them credit for
  • Whatever path you're on, keep building a portfolio, work samples convince people faster than any qualification does

Where I'd Land On This

Neither skills nor a degree wins this argument outright, and honestly, anyone who tells you it's a clean answer is probably trying to sell you something. What actually gets you hired is being useful for the specific role you're applying for. Sometimes that means a degree. Sometimes it means a portfolio and a willingness to prove yourself in the interview. Most of the time, it's a mix of both, plus a bit of timing and effort that no chart can really capture.

article_title: Resume vs LinkedIn Profile: What Recruiters Really Check First

meta_keyword: career advice, job search, resume tips, linkedin optimization, recruiter insights, job market trends

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
A recruiter once told me something that kind of stuck with me for years after — she said she'd already checked my LinkedIn before she even bothered opening my resume. At the time I thought that was odd. Wasn't the resume supposed to be the main thing? Turns out no, not really, not anymore.

If you're applying for jobs right now, you already know you need both. Fine. But here's what most people get wrong — they treat these two things like they're the same document, just in two different places. They're not. A recruiter doesn't read them the same way, doesn't look for the same things, and honestly doesn't even open them in the order you'd expect.

So let's actually get into it.

Why This Mix-Up Even Happens

Most people build their LinkedIn as basically a copy of their resume. Same job titles, same "responsible for managing X" type lines, nothing that actually sounds like them. And that's the problem right there — a lot of genuinely good candidates get skipped over just because their online profile reads like a template nobody bothered to personalize.

One document filters you out. The other one decides whether someone even wants to reach out in the first place. Different jobs, different documents.

Resume vs LinkedIn — Side by Side

Factor Resume LinkedIn Profile
Main job Gets you shortlisted for one role Builds credibility over time
Format Fixed PDF, one version at a time Always changing, always live
Who's reading The hiring manager, for this job only Recruiters, old colleagues, clients, basically anyone
Tone Formal, numbers-heavy More personal, more story
Length Kept to 1-2 pages However long you want, really
Read first in 2026 Usually not Usually yes
How often updated Only when applying somewhere Constantly, almost like a running log

That "read first" row is honestly the whole point of this article, if I'm being blunt about it.

What Recruiters Actually Check on a Resume

By the time a recruiter has your resume open, they've mostly already decided you're worth a look. So now they're not reading line by line — they're scanning for a handful of specific things.

What they check Why
Keywords matching the JD ATS software filters on this before a human even sees it
Numbers, not vague claims "grew revenue 22%" lands better than "handled sales"
Progression Are you growing, or just moving sideways job to job
Layout A messy resume, fair or not, reads as a messy person
Employment gaps They'll ask about it eventually, so don't try to hide it

One thing that's changed a lot lately — most companies now run resumes through AI-assisted ATS before anyone human looks at it. And these systems aren't dumb keyword counters anymore, they actually understand context. So the old trick of jamming buzzwords everywhere doesn't really work like it used to.

What Recruiters Actually Check on LinkedIn

This part's different. There's no real checklist for LinkedIn, it's more of a gut impression thing.

What they check Why
Photo and banner People judge this in like 2-3 seconds, whether we admit it or not
Headline If it's just your job title, you're wasting the space
About section Sounds like a real person, or copy-pasted from somewhere
Activity Are you actually around, or is this account basically dead
Recommendations Someone else vouching for you carries weight
Endorsed skills Adds a layer of proof beyond what you say about yourself
Mutual connections Trust builds faster when there's already some overlap

Something a lot of job seekers don't realize — recruiters are now leaning on LinkedIn's own AI search and summary features to shortlist people before sending a single message. So if your profile's thin or hasn't been touched since 2021, you could get filtered out of a role you never even knew existed.

Don't Make Them Twins

I know this sounds like it goes against the "keep everything consistent" advice you've probably heard a hundred times. But consistency just means the facts line up — titles, dates, companies. It doesn't mean the writing has to be identical.

Resume version:

"Led a team of 6 to deliver a product redesign that cut customer complaints by 30%."

LinkedIn version:

"Complaints kept piling up that quarter and at some point I just couldn't keep ignoring it. Grabbed five people from the team, we tore apart the user flow from scratch — took about three months, a lot of it messier than I'd like to admit. But by the end complaints were down 30%, and it's still one of the projects I bring up when people ask what I'm proud of."

Same achievement, told two different ways, for two different audiences. Both are true. Both work.

Mistakes People Are Still Making

  • Resume photo (or worse, LinkedIn photo) that's basically five years out of date
  • Sending the identical resume to every single application, no tailoring at all
  • LinkedIn headline that's literally just your job title and nothing else
  • Never touching the "Open to Work" settings, so you're invisible to recruiter search
  • Ghost profile — zero posts, zero comments, nothing for months on end
  • Skipping recommendations because "they're not that important" (they are, now more than ever)

The Way I'd Sum This Up

Your resume is answering one question: can this person actually do the job. Your LinkedIn is answering a slightly different one: do I want to talk to this person, and can I trust what they're telling me.

There's more competition than ever right now, a lot of it AI-assisted applications flooding every posting. Which honestly makes the human stuff stand out more, not less — real stories, actual numbers, a personality that comes through instead of a generic template.

Before You Hit Apply

  • Resume actually tailored to this job, not the same one you send everywhere
  • LinkedIn headline says more than just your title
  • At least a couple of recent recommendations up
  • Photo's current, looks like you look now
  • Resume and LinkedIn facts match, even if the tone doesn't
  • You've posted or commented on something in the last month

Get this right and you stop being just another name in the pile.

Curious — does anyone actually check your resume first these days, or is it LinkedIn every time? Let me know in the comments.

contents.content:
I get asked this a lot — "which resume template should I actually use?" And honestly, there's no single right answer. It depends on what job you're going for, how much you want to show off visually, and whether the company you're applying to even bothers reading past the ATS screening. One template that a lot of people gravitate toward lately has a dark header, a round profile photo up top, skill bars running down the side, and a two-column body underneath it. That's the one I want to talk about here.

If you've seen it before and wondered whether it's worth using, or you're just trying to figure out if it fits your field, this should clear things up.

Breaking Down the Layout

The template is really just two zones stitched together. Nothing fancy, but it's laid out in a way that makes sense once you see it in front of you.

Section Where It Sits What Goes In It
Header Full-width, top Name, designation, location, phone, email, website
Left Sidebar Left column Skills with progress bars, Languages, Social Links, Hobbies
Main Content Right column Profile Summary, Work Experience, Internships, Education, Certifications

What I like about this setup is that it gives you room to include the extra stuff — languages, hobbies, social links — without it feeling like you're cramming things into a corner just to fit them in.

What Actually Sets It Apart

A few small design choices make this template stand out from the usual plain-text resume:

  • Skill bars next to each listed skill — instead of just naming a skill, you can show roughly how good you are at it (Intermediate, Proficient, Advanced, that sort of thing)
  • A dotted timeline running through Work Experience, Internships, and Certifications, so it reads a bit like a story instead of a list
  • One accent color used consistently across headers and icons — small detail, but it makes the resume look put-together rather than thrown together
  • A proper spot for social links, which honestly gets left out of a lot of templates even though recruiters do check LinkedIn and GitHub

Who Should Actually Go For This One

Not every template works for every job, and this one's no exception. Some fields respond well to a bit of visual flair, others really don't.

Candidate Type Good Fit? Why
Retail / Sales Professionals Yes The skill bars make your strengths easy to scan at a glance
Freshers / Students Yes Internships and education actually get proper visibility instead of being buried
Designers / Creative Roles Yes The layout itself doubles as a small demonstration of design sense
Corporate / Finance Roles Not really These industries usually expect something more conservative and text-heavy
Senior Management Roles Not really Timeline-style templates tend to read as junior to mid-level

Now, About ATS — Will It Even Get Read?

This is the part people worry about most, and fair enough. A resume can look great and still get chewed up by an applicant tracking system if it's not built carefully.

Element ATS-Safe? Note
Two-column layout Mostly Older ATS software can occasionally scramble the reading order
Skill progress bars Somewhat risky Type out the actual skill level in words too, don't rely on the bar alone
Icons for contact info Usually fine Just make sure the text sits right next to the icon, not inside it
Profile photo Depends Normal practice in India, but some international recruiters prefer no photo at all

If the company you're applying to is a large corporate setup, it doesn't hurt to keep a plainer, single-column resume on standby too. Better safe than filtered out before a human even looks at it.

A Few Things Worth Doing (and Avoiding)

Some of this is common sense, but it's easy to overlook once you're deep in template customization mode:

  • Keep the skills section tight — only what's actually relevant to the role you're applying for
  • Add real numbers to your work experience wherever you can, even something like "grew monthly sales by 10%" changes how a line reads
  • Stick to professional social links only, this isn't the place for a personal Instagram
  • Don't try to fit every section you can think of, a resume with too much going on stops being readable
  • Don't guess at your skill bar levels just to look good, recruiters notice inconsistency between what you claim and how you answer in an interview
  • Keep certification and work dates in one consistent format throughout

Timeline Template vs a Plain One — Side by Side

Factor Timeline Template Simple/Minimal Template
Visual Appeal High Lower
ATS Safety Medium High
Best For Retail, creative, entry-level roles Corporate, government, traditional industries
Customization Options High — colors, bars, icons Limited
Recruiter Scan Time Fast, guided by visuals Fast, but plainer

Where I'd Land On This

If you're in retail, sales, design, or you're a fresher still building out your work history, this template genuinely does a good job of making a thin resume look complete and a strong one look even better. But if you're eyeing a corporate or finance role, or applying somewhere known for being conservative about hiring formats, I'd lean toward something simpler instead.

At the end of the day, the best template isn't the one that looks the most polished on screen — it's the one that gets your actual experience across clearly, without getting in its own way.

contents.content:
Have you ever felt that everyone else is moving forward in their career while you still feel confused about your future? This feeling is more common than you might think, whether you're a fresher or someone with five years of experience. A successful career doesn't require a perfect plan. It requires making small, consistent decisions in the right direction. In this post, we'll look at practical ways to make better career decisions.

Why career confusion happens

Most people feel stuck in their careers because of these:

  • They don't know their actual strengths.
  • They choose safe option and ignore the actual interest.
  • Family or society pressure ends up driving major decisions.
  • They stop upgrading skills after getting a job.

If any of these points sound familiar, you're not alone. Many people face the same challenges.

5 practice steps for career planning

Step What to Do Time Needed
1. Self-Assessment Write down your skills, interests, and values, then analyze them honestly 1-2 weeks
2. Market Research Check the demand and growth potential of your target field 1 week
3. Skill Gap Analysis Compare your current skills against what the role actually requires 3-4 days
4. Build an Action Plan Plan courses, certifications, or projects to close the gap 1 week
5. Execute and Review Track progress every few months and adjust course Ongoing

This process not work perfectly in first try because career growth is rarely a straight line.

Key Skills Across Different Career Fields

Field Core Technical Skills Essential Soft Skills
Software Development Coding, Debugging, System Design Problem-solving, Patience
Digital Marketing SEO, Content, Analytics Tools Creativity, Communication
Design (UI/UX) Wireframing, Figma, Prototyping Empathy, Attention to detail
Sales & Business Dev CRM Tools, Negotiation Confidence, Listening skills
Government/Sarkari Jobs Subject Knowledge, Exam Strategy Discipline, Consistency
Teaching/EdTech Subject Expertise, Digital Tools Patience, Explaining skills

Technical skills are important, but strong communication, teamwork, and problem solving skills often help people grow faster in their careers.

Common Resume and Interview Mistakes

A lot of candidates lose out on good opportunities because of small, avoidable mistakes.

Mistake What It Causes Fix
Sending the same generic resume everywhere Recruiters don't see relevance to the role Customize your resume for each job
ATS-unfriendly formatting Resume gets rejected by the system before a human sees it Use a simple, clean, ATS-friendly format
Giving memorized, rehearsed answers Comes across as inauthentic Share real examples and personal stories
Not following up after interviews Recruiter simply forgets you Send a short, polite thank-you email
Avoiding salary discussions You end up accepting a lower package Do market research and negotiate confidently

The Most Underrated Career Skill

  • Share work-related updates or insights on LinkedIn regularly
  • Leave thoughtful comments on posts from people in your industry
  • Join alumni groups and professional communities
  • Attend events or webinars, even the online ones
  • Stay in touch with colleagues and classmates

A Realistic Career Growth Timeline

Many people expect quick results, but career growth usually takes time.

Time Period What to Expect
0-1 Year In learning phase, focus on building a solid foundation
1-3 Years Skills sharpen and confidence starts building
3-5 Years Specialization and leadership opportunities start opening up
5+ Years Clear direction and stability in your career path

Do's and Don'ts to Keep in Mind

Do:
  • Learn at least one new skill or concept every month
  • Keep your portfolio or resume updated
  • Actively seek feedback and act on it
  • Treat financial planning as part of career planning
Don't:
  • Fall into the comparison trap
  • Don't choose a job based only on salary also choose accordign to career growth opportunity.
  • Stop learning once you land a job
  • Don't ignor burnout,break is also important.

Final Thoughts

Your career is not a race. Everyone grows at their own pace. It's a continuous journey where every step teaches you something new. Don't compare your joourney with another because every one have different mindset and starting point.
